Ho míš-eyá hená waŋblí čha, míš anúŋkȟasaŋ éyapi čha héčheča hená wóilagwičhawayiŋ kta škhé.
If I help them somehow, then they said that they would help me.
Hená tókhel wačhíŋwičhawayiŋ kte eháŋtaŋhaŋš, ómakiyapi kta kéyapi.
Because these birds live in a sacred way like that.
Ho čha hená héčhel wakȟáŋyaŋ ziŋtkála kiŋ lená úŋpi čha.
Nobody kills them for no reason.
Tuwéni otúyačhiŋ wičhákte šni.
Nobody makes use of them for no reason.
Tuwéni otúyačhiŋ wóilagwičhaye šni.
So that’s all.
Čha héčhegla.
It would be good for us Natives who are part of this religion to pray to God as much as we can, but we don’t feel like doing that.
Ikčé wičháša wóčhekiye oúŋpȟapi kiŋ hená tókhel okíhi Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka čhéuŋkiyapi waštéka, tkȟá ečhúŋ-uŋkápiŋpi.
For that reason, all of the societies are weak.
Hé uŋ etáŋhaŋ, okȟólakičhiye oyás’iŋ húŋkešni.
A long time ago when I was a little girl, I went to school with a young woman.
Eháŋni wimáčhiŋčala k’uŋ héhaŋ, wikȟóškalaka waŋ kičhí wabláwa.
So a long time ago we first went to school, so at that time some were old, but just then they were going to school for the first time.
Čha eháŋni tȟoká waúŋyawapi čha, héhaŋ húŋȟ waníyetu ótapi éyaš, lé nakéš otȟókaheya wayáwapi čha.
Because this was kindergarden.
Lé kindergarden kiŋ lé é čha.
So this young woman was maybe older than 20, but just then she was going to school there.
Čha wikȟóškala kiŋ lé tókhi wikčémna núŋm isáŋm iyáye k’éyaš nakéš héčhiya owáyawa.
So then I just was ten years old.
Čha héhaŋ iŋšé miyé waníyetu mawíkčemna.
And so this young girl studied there, and finally she didn’t go to school, and so they said that, and because of that they said she was sick.
Yuŋkȟáŋ wikȟóškalaka kiŋ lé hél wayáwa na, haŋkéya wayáwa šni yuŋkȟáŋ, oyákapi na, khúža kéyapi čha.
They say that they took her eastward, there to a hospital.
Wiyóhiyaŋpatakiya éyayapi kéyapi, héčhiya okhúže thípi waŋ ektá.
They would cure her so they say they took her there.
Asníyaŋpi kta čha éyayapi kéye.
On account of that, if those children of ours are going to be good somehow, this is the one tradition from which they should be good.
Héčhiyataŋhaŋ uŋ, uŋkítȟawakȟaŋyežapi kiŋ hená tókhel waštépi kta héčiŋ wičhóȟ’aŋ waŋží etáŋhaŋ waštépi kta iyéčhetu kiŋ hé lé é.
So she didn’t come back for a good long time, but they said that, and that those doctors couldn’t let her come back.
Hó yuŋkȟáŋ líla tȟéhaŋ glí šni éyaš, oyákapi na, wašíču wakȟáŋ kiŋ hená gličúyapi okíhipi šni kéyapi.
Because she was very sick.
Líla khúža čha.
And so her mother and father often got there to see her, and so they said that for some time, and they said that whenever that young girl had reached that time of the month, it scared her.
Yuŋkȟáŋ húŋku na atkúku kiŋ eyášna ektá waŋyáŋg ípi yuŋkȟáŋ, otóhaŋl oyákapi na, wikȟóškalaka kiŋ hé toháŋ tȟaŋkál yaŋkíŋ kta čháŋna šna, nihíŋčiya kéye.
So she often told the doctors, and whenever it was like that, she got sick, and she didn’t know what to do.
Čha wašíču wakȟáŋ kiŋ eyášna owíčhakiyakiŋ na, tóhaŋ héčheča kta čháŋšna, khúžiŋ na, tak-tókȟuŋ kte kiŋ slolkíye šni.
It was said that she was becoming powerful.
Líla waš’áka áya kéye.
So when she was going to be like that, it is said that they strapped her down with a rope.
Čha tóhaŋ héčheča kte háŋtaŋhaŋš, ikȟáŋyaŋ égnakapi čhíŋ kéye.
And so she probably went crazy, whenever they often also completely shut the door on her.
Čhaŋkhé eyášna áta thiyópa kiŋ hená kȟó aónatȟakapi čháŋšna, átaya tókhi gnaškíŋyaŋ načhéče.
She went crazy, and usually she totally broke the chair or even the table, too.
Gnaškíŋyiŋ našná, átaya owákaŋyaŋke naíŋš wágleyutapi hená é kayéš kȟó áta kawéȟweǧa.
And so finally it’s said that they tied her down with chains.
Čhaŋkhé haŋkéya máza ikȟáŋyaŋ gnákapi kéye.
Finally they realized that it was progressing, and so they say that she grew long fur.
Héčhena haŋkéya líla áya čha ablézapi yuŋkȟáŋ, lé há kiŋ hiŋšmá áya kéyapi.
The priest from Washington D.C. who looks over Natives, called Father Ketcham, he held a big meeting and he held a very big mass.
Washington D.C. etáŋhaŋ Wičháša Wakȟáŋ Ikčé Wičháša awáŋwičhayaŋke kiŋ, Father Ketcham ečíyapi kiŋ, omníčiye waŋ tȟáŋka yuhá na wičhóȟ’aŋ tȟáŋka ȟča él kȟoyágya yuhá.
It grew like it was mouse fur, and so they kept watching over her, and so eventually she couldn’t speak.
Lé itȟúŋkala híŋ kiŋ héčha s’e áya čhaŋkhé, awáŋyaŋg khuwápi yuŋkȟáŋ, haŋkéya iyá okíhi šni.
So they say that she was really scared.
Čha líla wókȟokipȟeka kéyapi.
Whenever the first month came, she was like that, around the time that her time of the month came.
Tóhaŋ wí waŋží ihúŋni čháŋšna, lé tȟaŋkál yaŋkíŋ kte wahéhaŋ šna, héčheča.
So around that time they usually put her aside, but eventually it was said that it was progressing”.
Hó čha wahéhaŋ šna gnákapi éyaš, haŋkéya líla áya kéye.
And that’s why she was always like that, tied up.
Na óhiŋniyaŋ kašká héčheča čha.
So those doctors, they went to the president, and they made an agreement, and maybe if her mom and dad agreed, they would give this woman medicine, and they say that they would put her to sleep.

Hó čha lé wašíču wakȟáŋ kiŋ lé tȟuŋkášilayapi ektá hená iyáyapi naháŋ, wóokiye lápi naháŋ, uŋgná húŋku na atkúku kiŋháŋ iyówiŋyaŋpi háŋtaŋhaŋš, wíŋyaŋ kiŋ lé pȟežúta k’úpi naháŋ, ištíŋmekhiyapi kta kéyapi.
They said that that way she would die in her sleep.
Ištíŋme kiŋ héčhena t’íŋ kta čha kéyapi.
Her mother and father talked to them, so they definitely couldn’t, but whenever they came to look over her, eventually she didn’t recognize them.
Húŋku na atkúku kiŋ owíčhakiyakapi čha, takómni tókhel okíhipi šni čha, waŋglág ípi khéš, haŋkéya iyéwičhakiye šni.
So in the end she became hairy all over.
Čha haŋkéya átaya hiŋšmá áya.
So they gave up.
Čha ayúštaŋpi.
On account of this, us Native people should let the kids take part in having their own way of life.
Héčhiyataŋhaŋ uŋ, Ikčé Wičháša wakȟáŋyeža wičhóuŋ yuhápi kiŋ hél ópȟewičhauŋkhiyapi kta iyéčhetu.
They gave up and it is said that they signed their names.
Ayúštaŋpi na čhažé oígwapi kéye.
So they put that young woman to sleep until she died.
Čha wikȟóškalaka hé ištíŋmekhiyapi na héčhena t’á škhé.
They say that that’s what was told.
Kéya oyákapi.
So maybe that girl walked like some of those old sort of men on the road, and they say those were wolves so it’s possible she was like that.
Čha hé tókhi wikȟóškalaka kiŋháŋ eháŋni táku wičháša eyá čhaŋkú ogná enágna ománipi na, hená šuŋmáyetupi škhé čha héčha načhéče.
They say that it’s said that maybe she became like that
Uŋgnáhelaka héčha hiŋglá kéya oyákapi.
That’s all.
Hó henákeča.
In the future with that alone will the kids grow up well.
Hečéla tȟokáta wakȟáŋyeža waŋží wašté ičháȟ úŋpi kte.
For you see, because a church is being built for them there, nobody can produce good things without a reason for it and nobody can have a good family without a reason for it.
Iŋčhíŋ hél líla wóčhekiye tȟáŋka wičhákičaǧapi kiŋ hé uŋ etáŋhaŋ, tuwéni otúyačhiŋ táku wašté ičháȟya okíhi šni na tuwéni otúyačhiŋ thiwáhe wašté yuhá kta okíhi šni.

Maybe more than about four weeks ago, we held a purification ceremony with a woman, but she was a white woman, so we held a purification ceremony with her, and so then she came out, and she said, “all your spirits were hanging around me so I couldn’t go outside, I sat there motionless.”

Lél héktakiya tókhi okó tópa séče isáŋmya heháŋn, wíŋyaŋ waŋ kičhí iníuŋkaǧapi éyaš, lé ská wíŋyaŋ héčha čha, kičhí iníuŋkaǧapi yuŋkȟáŋ, héhaŋ lé glinápȟiŋ na, hé, “átaya wanáǧi nitȟáwa kiŋ hená aháŋnažiŋ makhúwapi čha, átaya iȟéyab iblábla owákihi šni, škaŋškáŋ šni maŋké k’uŋ,” eyá čha.
“Maybe they do that, if something’s wrong with you.”
“Uŋgná tónikheča héči, hé uŋ héčhuŋpi k’uŋ.”

And so maybe it was a week from then that her husband talked, and he said, “my wife usually sees a doctor, and then she talked to him, and she went to the doctor or to a hospital, and he asked her to have herself see him.

Hó yuŋkȟáŋ hetáŋ tókhi okó waŋžíča yuŋkȟáŋ, hiŋgnáku kiŋ oyákiŋ na hé, “mitȟáwiču kiŋ lé wašíču wakȟáŋ waŋ eyášna waŋyáŋkiŋ naháŋke, okíyakiŋ na, wašíču wakȟáŋ waŋží ektá naíŋš okhúže thípi waŋží ektá yíŋ na, waŋyáŋg-ič’íčhiye-ši.
Because something was in her stomach.”
Thezí mahél táku waŋ úŋ čha.”
And so eventually she was becoming really sick, and so they brought her to the hospital, and so they said that she had a tapeworm in her stomach.
Ho yuŋkȟáŋ haŋkéya líla khúža áya čhaŋkhé, okhúže thípi ektá aípi yuŋkȟáŋ, thezí ektá waglúla waŋ úŋ kéyapi.
For you see, wherever God’s word is, only in that is one able to grow up with good things.
Iŋčhíŋ tuktél Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka oíye kiŋ yaŋké háŋtaŋš ečéla él táku wašté ičháǧa okíhi.
And so it’s said that she passed a lot of them near there, too.
Čhaŋkhé kaísakhibya líla óta ihéwičhaya kéye, nakúŋ.
And so she was really sick in that way.
Yuŋkȟáŋ héčhetu waŋná líla khúža kéye.
She got back, and she had a dream, and so she said that.
Glí na, iháŋbla yuŋkȟáŋ, heyá keye.
There was a very low human voice that said, “we will kill you.”
Wičháho waŋ líla hó hukhúčhiyela čha, heyá kéye, “uŋníktepi kte ló,” eyá kéye.

And so they scared her half to death, so there they called me, so I said something to her, I said, “if there is a thing that is living in your stomach, it will die, and so that’s why you’ve been sick.”
Čhaŋkhé tȟaŋságt’eyapi čha, léčhiya makíyuȟlapi čha, owákiyakiŋ na, “hé táku čha thezí mahél ní uŋ héči, hé é čha waŋná t’íŋ kta čha hé uŋ, nikhúža-he kštó,” epȟé čha.
I said, “go praying hard.
“Š’agyáhaŋ wačhékiyiŋ yé.
And don’t think you’re going to die.”
Na nit’íŋ kta kéčhiŋ šni yé,” epȟé.
Anyways it’s said that you will get better.
Éšéš aníčisni kta kéya yé.
I said, “you will definitely get better.”
“Tókša ečhél iníyayiŋ kte kštó,” epȟé.
And I addressed her husband and I said, “smudge in your house, and take some of those regular waters, and if she’s going to drink it, smudge over it, and pray over it, and give it to her.
Na hignáku kiŋ wakȟíŋ na, “thiyówazilyiŋ naháŋ, ikčéya lé mní kiŋ léčha čha ičú naháŋ, yatkíŋ kte háŋtaŋhaŋ, azílyatȟuŋ naháŋ, awáčhekiyiŋ na, k’ú we.
For that reason, my relatives, you should let your children participate in it.
Hé uŋ etáŋhaŋ, mitákuyepi, ničhíŋčapi kiŋ hél opȟéwičhayakhiyapi kta iyéčheča.
She’ll definitely get better in this way,”
Tókša ečhél iyáyiŋ kte kštó,” epȟé.
And so it’s said that he would do that.
Yuŋkȟáŋ héčhuŋ kta kéye.
He prayed over the water, and he smudged over it, and then he gave it to her, and so in this way her stomach was really hurting her, and she was all doubled up in pain.
Mní awáčhekiyiŋ na, azílyiŋ naháŋke, k’ú yuŋkȟáŋ, léčhel líla áta thezí kiŋ yazáŋ na, átaya peháŋ-haŋ kéye.

And so they took her back to the hospital, and so I guess they made her wait, so she was actually really sick, but she laid waiting, and so she wanted to use the restroom, and so they gave them a toilet in the bed, so it was that that she would use, so they gave it to her, and so she expelled all of what were those tapeworms.

Čhaŋkhé hétkakiya okhúže thípi ektá aípi yuŋkȟáŋ, itȟó él apȟékhiyapi čha, héčheya líla khúže éyaš, apȟé ȟpáya-haŋ yuŋkȟáŋ, tȟaŋkáye kíniča čhaŋkhé, lé oyúŋke él šna oíheye waŋ wičhák’upi čha, hé é čha úŋ kta čha k’úpi yuŋkȟáŋ, lé waglúla waŋ hé é čha áta ihéya kéye.
And she expelled them which were really small.
Na čikčík’ala kȟó átaya ihéwičhaya kéye.
She expelled them and then she got better from her stomach which was really badly hurting with cramps
Ihéwičhayiŋ naháŋke al’áta lé thezí yazáŋ nathíbthipe k’uŋ hé akísni kéye.
And so he said, “we didn’t treat you, evidently somehow you did it, you know you passed the tapeworms.
Čhaŋkhé “wašíču wakȟáŋ kiŋ aphíuŋniyaŋpi šni, tókheškhe ečhánuŋ wélakȟa, waglúla kiŋ ihéyaye k’uŋ” eyá kéye.

And so she said, “yeah, because I waited a really long to so for that reason finally my stomach was sick” so he said, “but you couldn’t have passed them without this medicine and yet you did anyways.”
Čhaŋkhé, “háŋ, ičhíŋ líla tȟéhaŋ awápȟe čha hé uŋ haŋkéya thezí mayázaŋ,” čha hé, “éyaš lé pȟežúta čhóla ihéyaya oyákihi šni škȟá héčhanuŋ k’uŋ,” eyá kéye.
So they sent her back, so she got home, and I told her that it was soft foods that she should eat.
Čha gličúyapi čha, thiyáta glí na, lé táku pȟaŋpȟáŋla hená é čha yul-wáši.
In that way she passed all the things in her stomach.
Héčhel lé thezí mahél táku úŋ kiŋ átaya ihékiya čha.
One year is 25¢.
Ómakȟa waŋžíča kiŋ hé ¢25.
That’s why there was nothing in her stomach.
Hé uŋ tákuni thezí mahél úŋ okíhi šni kéye.
So I told her to do that and so all of a sudden she called me again.
Hó čha héčhuŋ-waši yuŋkȟáŋ áta uŋgnáhelaka akhé mas’ámakipȟapi.

Maybe about a week ago, she called me, and then she just had stuff happen to her again, so her chest was hurting too, so I addressed her husband, and I said, “take her to the hospital again, maybe she has a stone in her stomach.”

Tókhi hékta okó k’uŋ héhaŋ, mas’ámakipȟapi naháŋke, akhé ečhéȟči wákhipȟa čha, átaya makhú kȟó yazáŋ čha, hiŋgnáku kiŋ wakȟíŋ na, “héktakiya okhúže thípi ektá áya yé, uŋgná íŋyaŋ waŋží thezí mahél úŋ séče kštó,” epȟé.
And so he arrived there with her like that so she lay waiting just like that.
Yuŋkȟáŋ léčhel aípi čha, héčheȟčiŋ apȟé ȟpáye.
And so she expelled that stone all on her own.
Yuŋkȟáŋ iyéčhiŋka íŋyaŋ kiŋ hé ihéya kéye.
She expelled that stone, so she became well again, and nowadays she’s gotten better.
Íŋyaŋ kiŋ hé ihéya čha, kaéčhel iyáyiŋ na, leháŋn waŋná akísni.
She’s gotten better but her stomach is still sensitive inside.
Akísni éyaš eháke thezí kiŋ naháŋȟči mahél pȟaŋpȟáŋla čha.
I think that she was eating just children’s food for a while.
Otóhaŋyaŋ hokšíčala tȟawóyute ečéla yúta-hiŋ kta képȟe.
When she get’s all better, then I say that I think that she will live healthy and smoothly.
Tókša kaéčhel iyáye kiŋháŋ, heháŋn okáblaya zaníya úŋ kta képȟa owákiyaka čha.
So I’m really happy about this.
Čha lé awíyuškiŋ laȟčake.
How else could a church be built for them but with that.
Uŋ wóčhekiye tȟáŋka wičhákičaǧapi kte lakȟáš.
That’s all.
Héčhegla.
Two months ago, one of my grandchildren was really sick.
Wí núŋpa k’uŋ héhaŋ, tȟakóžala waŋ líla khúže.
She’s one of my grand-grandchildren.
Isáŋm tȟakóža héčha čha.
She was as sick as could be so it’s said that they brought her to a hospital
Toháŋn okíhilaka khúža čha okhúže thípi ektá aípi kéye.
And so her inner ear was hurting and she was really going crazy and so it’s said that the doctor said, “it’s a hole inside your ear.”
Yuŋkȟáŋ lél núŋǧe opȟáya yazáŋ na, áta t’eblézešni čhaŋké, wašíču wakȟáŋ kiŋ hé eyá kéye, “lé núŋǧe mahél oȟlóka waŋ” eyá kéye.
So he said, “but we can’t treat you, maybe when we treat her, she won’t be able to hear, from then on.”
Čha, “éyaš aphíuŋyaŋpi uŋkókihipi šni k’uŋ, uŋgná aphíuŋyaŋpi kiŋháŋ, naȟ’úŋ okíhi kte šni, ho hetáŋ” eyá kéye.
And so my granddaughter was scared and they brought her here.
Čhaŋké tȟakóža kiŋ nihíŋčiyiŋ na lé isáŋm tȟakóžala kiŋ ahípi.
They brought her here, and they asked me to cure her, and so me myself I can’t do any miraculous acts, just Creator does those things.
Ahípi na, aphíye-mašipi čha, miyé tákuni wakȟáŋ waȟ’áŋ owákihi šni, iŋšé Tȟuŋkášila hená ečhúŋ.
Maybe then it will be proper that God’s strength is given to us.
Uŋgnáheȟčiŋ Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka wówaš’ake uŋk’úpi kta iyéčheča.

And so then they brought her here, so I filled a pipe with tobacco, and I prayed, and I took my daughter, and I blew all the smoke into her ear, and I said, “you will surely get better, granddaughter.”
Yuŋkȟáŋ čha lél ahípi čha, čhaŋlí owápaǧi na, lé wačhéwakiyiŋ naháŋ, tȟakóža kiŋ iwáču na, núŋǧe ektá átaya šóta obláblu na, “hó tókša tȟakóža aníčisni kte kštó.
Whenever they do that, they get well from those things.”
Lená léčhuŋpi čháŋšna hená uŋ akísnipi,” čha epȟé.

So then recently her mother told me something, and my granddaughter took her great-granddaughter all back to the doctor, and so the hole that they said had been in her ear healed up, and there was no problem at all, so they asked me if I did that, so I said, “you know things are like that through you all praying.”

Ho čha waŋná lečhálakel toháŋn húŋku kiŋ omákiyakiŋ na, mitȟákoža kiŋ isáŋm tȟakóžakpaku kiŋ áta héktakiya wašíču wakȟáŋ ektá aí, yuŋkȟáŋ lé núŋǧe oȟlóka kéyapi k’uŋ hé naókhiyutȟiŋ na, átaya tókheča šni čha tókheškhe héčhamuŋ héči, imáyuŋǧapi k’uŋ čha, “ičhíŋ wačhéyakhiyapi uŋ hená héčheča k’uŋ,” epȟé.
So instead nowadays she is running around without any health issues.
Čha ée leháŋn tókhečašniyaŋ oíŋyaŋka-he.
So back then she always had a fever, and she was sickly, and so nowadays she’s not sick at all, so now she talks too, and she’s running around.
Čha eháŋni ókowaŋžila kȟátiŋ naháŋ, khušyáhaŋ úŋ yuŋkȟáŋ, líla leháŋn áta tókhečala šni čha, kȟóš waŋná iyíŋ na, oíŋyaŋka-he.
Yup.

Waŋná tȟaníǧa kiŋ hé íŋš áta yužážapi na, tȟašúpa kiŋ húŋȟ hená paéčhiyapi naháŋ, owóhe waŋží él čhéǧa waŋží ektá hená piȟyápi naháŋ, š’éš’eya ǧéǧeya otkéyapi čha, hená čhosyápi čha.
If it’s dry, those make you feel bad, so they dry them like that, and they put them inside.
Púze háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená ošíče šni čha, héčhel pusyápi na, mahél iyéyapi.

And some of the intestines wind around so they blow into them, and they tie them to each other on both sides, so they blow on them that way, and when they’re still dry they put them inside, and it’s a stick that they wind them around, and then they roast them.
Ho na tȟašúpa kiŋ hé íŋš húŋȟ kšaŋkšáŋ čha, hená póǧaŋpi na, itȟánuŋg iyákaškapi čha, héčhel póǧaŋpi na, héčhena púze čháŋšna, iyáyapi naháŋ, hená čháŋ čha kaíyapehaŋpi naháŋš čheúŋpapi.
They roast them over a fire and eat it.
Pȟéta kiŋ iwáŋkab čheúŋpapi na hé yútapi.
And they also punch a hole in the intestine, and when they stick tallow inside it there, they cook it, so it tastes really good.
Na tȟačháǧu kiŋ hé íŋš paȟlókapi na, héčhiya wašíŋkčeka mahél iyéyapi čháŋš, čhéuŋpapi čha, líla oyúl wašté.

And they dig up that liver, and they throw it onto live coals, and they throw the whole liver right in there, and they pile live coals on it, and whenever they roast it really well in the ashes, they eat the sliced up ones, if they didn’t cook it badly like that.

Na tȟaphí kiŋ hé íŋš makȟá k’ápi na, pȟetáǧa ektá oíȟpeyapi na, lé tȟaphí kiŋ lé áta héčhi mahél oíȟpeyapi na, pȟetáǧa akšúpi na, áta yuphíya čhok’íŋpi čháŋšna, ikčéya wasléslel ičú yútapi na, ošíče šni héčhel iȟ’áŋpi háŋtaŋhaŋš.
And they cut up the heart, and they dry it like that, and if they’re about to cook it, they take it down, and they take the cut up parts, and boil it.
Na tȟačháŋta kiŋ hé íŋš wasléslečapi na, héčhel pusyápi čha, iȟ’áŋpi kte háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená yuȟpápi na, tókhel wasléslečapi hená ičúpi na, iyóȟpeyapi.

Or they say that they turn some of the tender meat inside out so it’s that meat that they cut into long skinny strips, and they tie the intestines that they turned inside out to each other, and they pour water on it.
Naíŋš ló kiŋ héčhena húŋȟ tȟaló ipáečhiya eyápi čha héčhel tȟaló čha háŋskeya sósopi na, tȟašúpa kiŋ lé paéčhiyapi kiŋ okhíyakaškapi na, mní okáštaŋpi.
They tie it several times, and whenever they cook it like that, they make soup with water in it, so they drink that, and they eat it all together.
Tónakiya hé iyákaškapi na, héčhel hená iyóȟpeyapi čháŋna šna, mní mahél úŋ kiŋ hená waháŋpi káǧapi čha, hená yatkáŋpi, na iyáyustag iyáksa yútapi.
And they even take the bones, and whenever they cut open the leg bones, they take fat from what’s called “bone marrow,” and they strike it off bread, and eat it.
Na hohú kiŋ hená é kayéš ičúpi na, hú hohú kiŋ hená kašléčapi čháŋšna, hená tȟačhúpa eyápi čha hená hetáŋ wígli hená ičúpi na, hená aǧúyapi ikášlutapi na, yútapi.
There are 150 people that live in the way of St. Joseph’s society and St. Mary’s society.
St. Joseph na St. Mary okȟólakičhiye úŋpi kiŋ átaya 150 henákečapi.

Or maybe whenever they pound the jerky that they made, they mix it with that, and they eat that, and they split open again and again the leg joints, and whenever they boil that, if fat comes from it, they skim all of it up, and they put it somewhere else, and they make it boil.

Naíŋš uŋgná pápa káǧapi kiŋ lená kapȟápi čháŋšna, ektá ičáhiyapi na, hé yútapi na, lé hohú ókhihe kiŋ hená kašléšlečapi na, hená piȟyápi čháŋšna, wígli kiŋ hená akáŋ hiyú háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená ál’ataya kaǧépi na, ipáyeȟ ognákapi na, héčhel ipíȟyapi.
So if there’s still no fat, they throw that on, and whenever they mix in some horsemint with it, they grease their hair with it.
Ho na ečhél wígli waníče háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená iȟpéyapi naháŋ, wígli kiŋ hená waȟpé waštémna ičáhiyapi čháŋšna, hená uŋ pȟehíŋ slakíyapi.
And they also boil and dry the taken the head, and the tongue and the jowl so it’s hard when winter comes but in some way they live through it.
Na pȟá kiŋ íŋš hé ičúpi na, tȟačhéži na iyóȟa kiŋ lená nakúŋ hená piȟyápi na, pusyápi čha, toháŋn waníyetu kiŋ theȟí k’éyaš, tókhel ní yaŋkápi kte.
They cook those things of theirs and in that way they sit with plenty of food.
Hená ikíȟ’aŋpi na íŋš héčhel owólyala s’e yaŋkápi.
And whenever they cookcorn dry in the sun too, they dry it, so they braid some of the corn to the core, and they dry it by hanging it, if they cook it.
Na wagmíza nakúŋ hená čhosyápi čháŋšna, pusyápi čha, húŋȟ wagmíza kiŋ héčhena čhoǧíŋ ikȟóyagya súŋpi na, ǧéǧeya pusyápi, toháŋn iȟ’áŋpi háŋtaŋhaŋš.

Usually after that they shake it off, and they make the others into dried sweet corn, so they cut them off, and they boil them and they boil them, so that they’re slighlty cooked, and whenever they throw them out flat on the table, they dry them, and they make dried sweet corn.

Naíŋš hé íyohakab šna yugnápi na, uŋmá hená íŋš waštúŋkala káǧapi čha, hená wagnápi naháŋ, iyóȟpeyapi naháŋ, líla špáŋšniyaŋ iyóȟpeyapi naháŋ, wágleyutapi akáŋ yubláya iȟpéyapi čháŋšna, hená pusyápi na hená waštúŋkala káǧapi.
So they store them away for winter.
Čha hená íŋš-eyá waní-waékignakapi.
Or squash.
Naíŋš wagmú.
So what they peel all up is the thick rind of a yellow squash, and they cut this squash into strips, and they also dry it out on a table just like that.
Wagmú zí čhaŋhá šóka hé é čha hená átaya kaskúskupi na, lé wagmú kiŋháŋ wasléslečapi na, íŋš-eyá héčhel wágleyutapi akáŋ pusyápi.
Or they cut one of those into long circular strips, and they take a leather cord, and string it in the middle, and when they spread it out with the hands, they let it dry like that.
Naíŋš waŋží hená íŋš átaya okáwiŋȟ wasósospi na, wíkȟaŋ waŋží ičúpi na, čhokáŋ oyázapi na, yubláyapi čháŋšna, hená héčhel pusyápi.
During this winter, Mr. and Mrs. Sleeping Bear were baptized and were married.
Lé waníyetu kiŋ él Mr. na Mrs. Sleeping Bear mniáwičhakaštaŋpi na wakȟáŋkičhiyuzapi.

So in those ways they make those things into food, or then if they plan on cooking those things for someone during winter, they pull their things up, and they set it cooking on the firepit, so it becomes nice and soft on its own.
Čha hená ečhékčhe wóyute káǧapi naíŋš, waŋná waníyetu ektá hená ikíȟ’aŋpi kte háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená yuákaŋ ikíkčupi na, hená očhéthi kiŋ hél akáŋ hená iȟ’áŋ glépi čha, iyéčhiŋkala lolópela.
So they never use up anything.
Čha hená tóhaŋni tákuni yusótapi šni.
And also they gather berries.
Na hená nakúŋ wóšpipi.
If it’s summer, then they gather berries, and they pick all those chokeberries, and they knock them down, and they dry them, and they stick them inside, too.
Blokétu háŋtaŋhaŋš, wóšpipi na čhaŋpȟá hená áta yušpípi na, kaškípi na, pusyápi naháŋ íŋš-eyá hená mahél iyéyapi.
When they lay down all the things that they flatten and flatten, it dries.
Áta yubláskaska hená égnakapi čháŋšna púze.
Or they take those berries and in the old days they had the children squeeze it out.
Naíŋš kȟáŋta kiŋ hená ičúpi na eháŋni iŋšé wakȟáŋheža kiŋ kȟáŋta hená yaškíl-wičhakhiyapi.
And if they threw the seeds to the side, then they let them dry without the seeds.
Na sú kiŋ hená ȟeyáb iyéyapi eháŋtaŋhaŋš, sú čhóla hená pusyápi.

But nowadays it’s just a pot, and so they throw them in the pot, and when it’s boiling, and if they all start to pop, often they ladle them out, and they throw the seeds to the side, and they still dry them.
Éyaš iŋšé leháŋn hená čhéǧa yuŋkȟáŋ čha, čhéǧa ektá oíȟpeyapi na, iyé toháŋn píǧiŋ na, áta napȟópe háŋtaŋhaŋ, šna kazépi na, sú kiŋ ȟeyáb iȟpéyapi na, héčhena hená pusyápi.
They dry them so they just are food.
Pusyápi čha iŋšé hená wóyute.
Whenever it’s winter, they make that food.
Waníyetu čháŋ hená wóyute káǧapi.
Eliza Rocking Bear and Joe Elk Boy’s child, and James Black Bear’s child, and Joshua Spotted Bear’s child, they were all baptized and then they died.
Eliza Rocking Bear na Joe Elk Boy čhiŋčá na James Black Bear čhiŋčá na Joshua Spotted Owl čhiŋčá waŋ mniáwičhakaštaŋpi na heháŋl t’ápi.
They cook it into a porridge.
Yužápi.
But in the old days there was no sugar, so if they made that food, they didn’t mix in a lot.
Éyaš iŋšé eháŋni čhaŋháŋpi waníča čha, wóyute kiŋ lená káǧapi háŋtaŋhaŋš, óta ičáhiyapi šni.
They didn’t do those things a long time ago, and they mix it with flour a long time ago, but there wasn’t any of that a long time ago, so they made pudding by using what was scraped hide.
Hená eháŋni héčhuŋpi šni na, eháŋni hená aǧúyapiblú ičáhiyapi éyaš, hená hé é čha waníče eháŋni čha, lé tȟahá kaȟ’úpi hená é čha uŋ wóžapi káǧapi.
And at that time nobody had just bread, so just recently white people crossed over the water and then they finally gave them flour and bacon and yeast and soap.
Na iŋšé heháŋn tuwéni aǧúyapi yuhá šni čha, iŋšé lená lečhála wašíču kiŋ ahíyuweǧapi heháŋn nakéš aǧúyapiblú na khukhúše wašíŋ na wínakapo na haípažaža kiŋ lená wičhák’upi.
But they didn’t know about those things so they didn’t use them.
Éyaš hená táku kiŋ slolyápi šni čha úŋpi šni.
But a long time ago those Lakota ate what was really good, and they didn’t just mix anything together.
Ho éyaš eháŋni Lakȟóta kiŋ hená táku itéšniyaŋ wašté čha hená yútapi na, tákuni ikčéya íčhičahiyapi šni.
And what they ate was deer and buffalo and small four-legged animals that they ate.
Na táku yútapi kiŋ hé tȟáȟča naíŋš tȟatȟáŋka na wahútopa čikčík’ala hená é tóna hená wičháyutapi.
Those are the things, they didn’t eat those other bad things.
Hená ée, táku uŋmá hená šíča čha yútapi šni.
But today the make everything all mixed together, and they make the Lakota eat those things, so they all are sick.
Ho tkȟá leháŋn táku k’éyaš, áta íčhižena káǧapi na, Lakȟóta kiŋ oyúlwičhakhiyapi čha, iyúha khúžapi.
They are infected with diseases and they can’t get better.
Wičhókhuže ečhéčapi na akísnipi okíhipi šni.
On January 9th, Red Deer Woman died.
Jan. 9 hé óštaŋ Tȟáȟča Lúta wiŋ t’é.
And from however they made that jerky is what they call pemmican, so that’s tallow that they make it by mixing it with.
Ho na hé tókhel pápa káǧapi kiŋ letáŋhaŋ wakápȟapi eyápi čha hená wašíŋkčeka čha, hená ičáhiyapi hé káǧapi.
And it’s pemmican, it’s jerky that they pound, and it’s chokecherry that they mix into it too, and it’s tallow and in that way they make pemmican, mixing it with it.
Ho naháŋ wasná čha hé íŋš pápa čha kapȟápi naháŋ, hé čhaŋpȟá čha hé íŋš-eyá íčhičahiyapi naháŋ, wašíŋkčeka na héčhel wasná káǧapi, íčhičahiya.
But nowadays nobody does that, they mix all those things with sugar.
Éyaš leháŋn tuwéni hená ečhúŋ šni, hená iyúha čhaŋháŋpi ičáhiyapi.
All those things that they make they mix with sugar, and it’s with a grinder that they grind those things.
Táku káǧapi kiŋ lená iyúha čhaŋháŋpi ičáhiyapi na, wíyukpaŋ čha uŋ hená yukpáŋpi.
In the old days it was just with some rocks that they ground those things with, and they ground them like that like it was a hammer.
Iŋšé hená eháŋni íŋyaŋ eyá gmigméla čha él akáŋ wakáškipi naháŋ, íŋyaŋ imás’iyapȟa s’eléčheča hená uŋ kaškípi.
But nowadays it’s all grinders, so they find it ground, and they throw it on the table, or it’s a drier so throughout the night they dry all of it, and they put it inside.
Éyaš leháŋn hená iyúha wíyukpaŋ yuŋkȟáŋ čha, hé yukpáŋ iyéyapi na, wágleyutapila kiŋ akáŋ iȟpéyapi naíŋš, wípusye yuŋkȟáŋ čha, haŋhépi ópta hená iyúha pusyápi na, mahél iyéyapi.
Nowadays people’s lives go really fast.
Iŋšé leháŋn wičhóuŋ kiŋ líla oȟ’áŋkȟo.
In the old days it was hard to make those things, so they made all those prayers, and they respectfully put those things inside.
Eháŋni hená iyótiyekiya hená káǧapi čha, hená iyúha wóčhekiye ečhúŋpi na, hená gluónihaŋyaŋ mahél iyékiyapi.
In that way the people didn’t go hungry.
Héčhel oyáte kiŋ akiȟ’áŋpi šni.
But nowadays the people live in a European way.
Éyaš leháŋn líla oyáte kiŋháŋ wašíču wičhóuŋ.
On January 14th, C. Little Elk died.
Jan. 14 hé óštaŋ C. Little Elk t’é.
So they go hungry or there are very bad diseases.
Čha akíȟ’aŋpi naíŋš líla wičhókhuže čha šíča.
I will talk more about this, but I can’t remember some things, they’re somethings today that I will talk about when I remember some of them again.
Ho lé isáŋm oblákiŋ kte éyaš, húŋȟ wéksuye šni, húŋȟ leháŋn čha hé toháŋn wéksuye kiŋ akhé húŋȟ oblákiŋ kte.
On February 24th, Alfred Black Bear’s son died.
Feb. 24 hé óštaŋ Alfred Black Bear čhiŋčá t’é.
Remember it in your prayers.
Wóčhekiye nitȟáwapi él kíksuya po.
So here now for the second time I will talk about how they made use of the hides they made.
Hó lé ičínuŋpa kiŋ lé tȟahá káǧapi kiŋ hé é naíŋš tókhel wóilagyapi kiŋ hená oblákiŋ kte.
So then if they killed the buffalo, they made it into food.
Ho waŋná pté ktépi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená wóyute káǧapi.
And they took the hide, that cow’s skin, and sinew lied along the neck, so they pulled it out, and they washed it, and they scraped it smooth, and they dried it by sticking it to a tree.
Ho na tȟahá kiŋ hé, ptebléška kiŋ hé há, yúzapi na, tȟahú kiŋ ognáyaŋ tȟakȟáŋ ȟpáya čha, hé yuslútapi naháŋ, yužážapi na, pak’óǧapi na, čháŋ waŋží kaíyaskabya pusyápi.
And they took that hide, and they scraped it until it was dry, and they stretched it by nailing it, and if they dried it they shaved the hair like that.
Na tȟahá kiŋ hé ičúpi na, áta kašképapi naháŋ, yuzíl okátaŋpi na, pusyápi háŋtaŋhaŋš, héčhel híŋ kiŋ hená katkúpi.
And whenever they finished shaving the hair, they’d turn it over and on the other side, the meaty side, they’d also shave the hair, and they’d peel off all the sinew or meat that was stuck to it.
Naháŋ hé toháŋn katkúpi yuštáŋpi ehátaŋhaŋš, yuptáŋyaŋ iȟpéyapi naháŋ, uŋmáčhiyataŋhaŋ, tȟaló ečhíyataŋhaŋ, íŋš-eyá áta katkúpi na, tȟakȟáŋ naíŋš tȟaló táku él iyáskape kiŋ hená iyúha kaȟláyapi.

And if they finished that, they went, and they applied brains to all the hide, and smeared it all on, and they wetted it, and so if it absorbed all that, then they took it, and they cleaned it, and they wrung it out, and they tied it to a sickle like that, and it was that that they softened by rubbing it.

Na hó yuštáŋpi hátaŋhaŋš, iyáyapi na, tȟahá kiŋ hé áta tȟanásula čha, iyúŋpi na, átaya ipátȟaŋtȟaŋpi na, yuspáyapi ho na toháŋn hé áta kakpá iyáye háŋtaŋhaŋš, ho heháŋn ičúpi na, yužážapi ho na, yuškíčapi ho na, hé pȟežíkakse héčheča čháŋ ektá iyákaškapi, na ho hé é čha uŋ yuȟúŋtapi.

They gently went rubbing it until it was soft, and they went around rubbing it until it was soft all around, and whenever they rubbed it until soft in the same way on both sides, it was like that, until it wasn’t hard anywhere, it was really fragile like that on both sides.
Iwáštegla yuȟúŋn áyapi na ohómni okáwiŋȟ yuȟúŋta-haŋpi na, itȟánuŋgya áta ákhilečhelya yuȟúŋtapi čháŋšna, héčheš tukténi suksúta šni, áta héčhel íyakhilečhelya pȟaŋpȟáŋla.
So they did that, and back then if that sinew was dry then they took it, and peeled it off, and it was those things that they took tearing lengthwise by hand, and they made it into twine.
Hó čha héčhuŋpi na, héhaŋ hé tȟakȟáŋ kiŋ hé púze háŋtaŋhaŋš, yuȟláya ičúpi na, ho hená é čha yuslél ičúpi na, haȟúŋta káǧapi.
They separated the sinew into strips, and they made a lot of them, and they laid it down, and it was with those that they beaded or made quillwork.
Tȟakȟáŋ kiŋ kazápi na, hená óta káǧapi ho na, hé égnakapi na, hená é čha uŋ áta pšitȟó kšúpi naíŋš, wóskapi pȟahíŋ óskapi.
During this winter, I arrived at Crow Creek with the Gospels, and I worked with Father Ambrose.
Lé waníyetu kiŋ él wótȟaŋiŋ wašté ečhíyataŋhaŋ Kȟaŋǧí Okhúte ektá waí na Father Ambrose kičhí wówaši ečhámuŋ.
And they also made small things out of the leftovers of the small bits of hide, and those are parfleche bags or knife cases, and they made small things in those sort of ways.
Na toháŋn hená akáŋn tȟahá čikčík’a hená akáb’iyaye kiŋ hená íŋš-eyá táku čikčík’ala káǧapi na, wókapȟaŋ naíŋš míyožuha na, héčhekčhekel táku čikčík’ala hená káǧapi.

And they took the cow’s tail, and they cut it open, and they dried it by setting it out flat, and tightening it so they peeled all the hair off of it, and in that way they embroidered about that much of it on the flat side with quillwork.

Na ptebléška siŋté kiŋ hé ičúpi na, pablázapi na, yubláya yut’íŋš pusyápi čha, hená áta híŋ kiŋ katkúpi naháŋ, héčhel pȟahíŋ óskapi blaskáya watókhetuya óskapi čháŋšna, ho hél wíyaka núŋm aíyakaškapi čha, hé wapȟégnaka ečíyapi.
And with the others they made dresses or hide shirts.
Na uŋmá kiŋ lená čhuwígnaka káǧapi naíŋš tȟahá ógle.

They called them Chiefs’ shirts, so they made those in that way, or they made leggings, hide leggings, or they made some leggings for women, and moccasins, or they dried others that were all different, until they were really stiff, and if it was dry, it was those that they cut, and made the pieces for a moccasin.

Wičháša itȟáŋčhaŋ tȟaógle eyápi čha héčheča káǧapi naíŋš húŋska, tȟahá huŋská, naíŋš eyá hé wíŋyaŋ tȟahúŋska naháŋ, háŋpa naíŋš, eyá há tȟókeča čha, hená átaya sagyéla pusyápi na, púze háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená é čha waksápi naháŋ, haŋpsíčhu káǧapi.
They make the sole of the shoe with it.
Sičhúha hená káǧapi.
Or maybe they make a drum with part of it.
Naíŋš uŋgná haŋké čhaŋčhéǧa káǧapi.
They also make something that’s useful in that way.
Íŋš-eyá táku héčhel wóilake uŋ káǧapi.
So they also take some of that untanned hide, and they cut it into thin long strips, and whenever they weave them very tightly, they make a rope.
Čha hé tȟahásaka kiŋ nakúŋ húŋȟ ičúpi naháŋ, sósopi naháŋ, yuspáyapi na, líla yut’ísya súŋpi čháŋšna, wíkȟaŋ káǧapi.
And it is that that they made rope with.
