Yuŋkȟáŋ čhaŋšáša kiŋ lé čhaŋkú lúta eyápi čha hé ogná Lakȟóta kiŋ mánipi kta kéye.
So kinnikinnick grows from Grandmother Earth.
Ho hé čhaŋšáša kiŋháŋ Uŋčí Makȟá etáŋ ičháǧe.
It grows from Grandmother Earth and they smoke kinnikinnick.
Uŋčí Makȟá etáŋ ičháǧiŋ naháŋ čhaŋšáša kiŋ lená hená úŋpapi.
Now in winter there’s a lot of snow, and around the time when there are blizzards, whenever they break off kinnikinnick, they say that that way it isn’t bitter.
Waníyetu waŋná líla osní na, iwóblu wahéhaŋ, čhaŋšáša kiŋ lená kaksápi čháŋšna, héčhel pȟá šni kéye.
I addressed them with prayer as regards families.
Thiwáhe ečhíyataŋhaŋ wóčhekiye yuhápi kta čhažéblate.
And so they broke off those branches, and they shaved the bark, and then underneath the bark there is pith stuck between it.
Ho čha čháŋ kiŋ hená kaksápi naháŋ, há kiŋ kak’óǧapi naháŋ, heháŋn hél iyókogna čhaŋhá kiŋ hél iyóȟlathe waŋží čhoǧíŋ čha ikȟóyake.
So it’s that that they take what it is, and that they shave it, and dry it, and cut it into strips, and he mixes this tobacco, and cuts it with a knife, and they smoke with that.
Čha hé é čha ičúpi na, kak’óǧapi na, pusyápi na, waksáksapi na, lé čhaŋlí ičáhiye čha iwákpaŋpi na, uŋ úŋpapi.
So it is that that they fill in the pipe and smoke.
Ho hé é čha čhaŋnúŋpa kiŋ lé él opáǧipi naháŋ úŋpapi.
So if they use that tobacco and they stuff it in the pipe, they make prayers as many times as those several times that they stuff that into the pipe.
Ho čha hé čhaŋlí kiŋ hé toháŋn ičúpi naháŋ, čhaŋnúŋpa kiŋ hé él opáǧipi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená tóna akhígle opáǧipi kiŋ hé iyéna wóčhekiye káǧapi.
So in that way Lakota people walk well and they won’t come with any sickness.
Ho héčhel Lakȟóta kiŋháŋ taŋyáŋ mánipi na wičhókhuže waŋžíni él hípi kte šni.
But I say that it is health and life that kinnikinnick is.
Tkȟá wičhózani na wičhóni kiŋ lená úŋ he čhaŋšáša kiŋ hé é epȟé.
And so nobody knew that, and so he dreamed just in that way, and they told him it, and it’s from Grandmother Earth and Creator.
Ho yuŋkȟáŋ hé tuwéni slolyé šni yuŋkȟáŋ, héčhuŋ-s’e ihámniŋ na, okíyakapi na, ho hé Uŋčí Makȟá etáŋ Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka ektá iyóȟlogya.
When you walk with that, you will make a good lifestyle like that.
Toháŋn hé luhá mayáni kiŋháŋ héčhel oúŋ waŋží wašté yakáǧiŋ kte.
It is said that in that way somehow you will ask for something from Creator and he will help you.
Héčhel Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka tókhel táku yakíla éyaš óničiyiŋ kta kéye.
And so he finally understood it just like that.
Ho čha hé héčhuŋ-s’e iŋšé hé waŋná wičháša kiŋ hé eháke okáȟniǧe.
We have the sacrament of marriage from the holy societies and it’s something to really think hard about.
Okȟólakičhiye wakȟáŋ etáŋhaŋ wakȟáŋkičhiyuzapi uŋyúhapi na é wówiyukčaŋ líla tȟaŋkíŋkiŋyaŋ.
He wrote a book so it’s with that that he would finally arrived there to Alaska, and so they told him that just like that.
Wówapi waŋ káǧa čha hé é čha ká Osní Makȟóčhe héčhiya čha hé eháke hé él ékihuŋni kta yuŋkȟáŋ, hé héčhuŋ-s’e okíyakapi.
They told him that in a dream.
Wóihaŋble él okíyakapi.
So he took it and it is said that he would understand it.
Ho čha hé ičú naháŋ abléziŋ kta kéye.
And so they told him it just like that then, so at the end of the book they will write that, the story.
Ho yuŋkȟáŋ hená héčhuŋ-s’e waŋná okíyakapi čha, ho hé eháke wówapi waŋ káǧapi kiŋ él oéhaketa hená él owápi kte, wičhóoyake kiŋ.
And so afterwards he told me that.
Yuŋkȟáŋ hé íyohakab hé omákiyake.
He wants Lakota people to live well, and the people drink, and get drunk too much, and he says they shouldn’t get lost in doing that.
Lakȟóta kiŋ taŋyáŋ úŋpi čhíŋ yuŋkȟáŋ, oyáte kiŋ sáŋm líla wayátkaŋpi na, itómnipi na, él éič’iktuŋwaŋpi šni kéye.
He says that he’s not happy.
Iyókiphi šni kéye.
He told me, it happened just like this when he told me, “so from now on I won’t be alive, but if I tell you these things, then even if I won’t live, I will help you.”
Kéya omákiyake, “ho čha letáŋ tȟokátakiya nakúŋ él waúŋ šni éyaš, táku kiŋ lená oláke háŋtaŋhaŋš, tókša él waúŋ šni éyaš, óčhičiyiŋ kte k’uŋ,” eyé.
And so it happened.
Yuŋkȟáŋ iyéčhetu.
So it’s hard but I will tell those things.
Čha othéȟike éyaš takómni hená é čha oblákiŋ kte.
St. Paul said, “but why is it that we don’t pay attention to it.
St. Paul heyá, “tkȟá tákowe čha él éuŋtuŋpi šni.
And I tell those things so that Lakota people will be wise.
Na uŋ Lakȟóta kiŋháŋ ksápapi kta čha hená obláke.
So that is all that I have to say about kinnikinnick.
Čha wahéhaŋyela hé čhaŋšáša kiŋ oblákiŋ kte.
If someone always has Creator in mind, their ways of doing things are good, that’s what I mean.
Tuwá Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka awáčhiŋ kiŋ táku wičhóȟ’aŋ wašté iyéyiŋ kte ló, hé wakȟé ló.
Look over Adam and Eve in the beginning.
Na otȟókahe ektá Adam na Eva kičhí iwáŋwičhayaŋka po.
And look at Mary with Joseph.”
Na Mary na Joseph kičhí iwáŋyaŋka po.
It would be good for us Native people to have one of the most important rites.
Wičhóȟ’aŋ tȟáŋka kiŋ waŋží ȟčiŋ ikčé wičháša uŋyúhapi waštéke.
A long time ago there were horse riders, or racers, or bull riders, and whenever they had a dance campsite, they also had a rodeo.
Leháŋl eháŋni šuŋk’ákaŋyaŋkapi, naíŋš khiíyaŋkapi, naíŋš hečhékčhe pteákaŋyaŋkapi naháŋ wačhí éwičhothi čháŋšna, nakúŋ lé rodeo yuhápi.
They made an arbor outside, and all the people went there together, and they often danced for several days there.
Tȟaŋkál waȟpé wakhéya káǧapi naháŋ, ho hél áta oyáte kiŋháŋ ptáyela hél yápi naháŋ, ho hél tónačhaŋšna wačhípi.
And at the same time they had a rodeo.
Na nakúŋ isákhibya rodeo yuhápi.
They rode bulls whenever, or they rode broncos, or they raced.
Čháŋna šna pteákaŋyaŋkapi naíŋš, šuŋgwátȟogla akáŋyaŋkapi naíŋš, khiíŋyaŋkapi.
They did all those things.
Hená iyúha héčhuŋpi.
And they had giveaways or in many ways they camped together there happily.
Na wíȟpeyapi naíŋš héčhekčhe hená oíyokiphiphiya éwičhothi.
But that was quite a sight and they had a lot of fun.
Éyaš líla wówaŋyaŋke na líla oíyokiphi yuhápi.
But I don’t know anything about the sundances.
Éyaš toháŋni wiwáŋyaŋg wačhípi hé é tákuni slolwáye šni.
They also danced for several days too, but I don’t know how they did it back then.
Hená íŋš-eyá heháŋl šna tónačhaŋ wačhípi éyaš, hé é tókhel ečhúŋpi kiŋ héhaŋ slolwáye šni.
But Lakota people often camped there together and have fun.
Ho éyaš Lakȟóta kiŋ hél ptáyela šna oíyokiphiya šna wičhóthi.
And so now we know several things: baptism, confession, confirmation, holy communion, annointing of the sick and annointing of the dead, and holy orders.

Na eyá táku tóna waŋná slol’úŋyaŋpi: mniákaštaŋpi, wakȟáŋ woglákapi, wičháyusutapi, Yútapiwakȟáŋ ičúpi, wičhókhuže čhewíčhakičičhiyapi na wičhát’a čhewíčhakičiyapi na, kȟaŋǧí káǧapi čhewíčhakičičhiyapi.
So maybe they just lived there together and shared food with each other.
Čha iŋšé hé uŋgnáhaŋšna hél iyúha ptáyela úŋpi naháŋ nakúŋ wólkičhiyapi.
So I’ve told about those things that I know.
Čha nakúŋ hená slolwáye čha obláke.
So those things are like that and our Savior said, “without me, you all won’t be able to succeed in doing anything.”
Hó lená héčhetu na Waníkiya uŋkítȟawapi kiŋ léčhel eyá: “Miyé čhóla tákuni oyákihipi kte šni.”
A long time ago Lakota people grew up in a Lakota way.
Eháŋni Lakȟóta kiŋháŋ lená Lakȟól wičhówičhaǧe.
So they lived being lectured in regards to those things.
Ho na lená úŋ wówahokuŋkhiye uŋk’úpi.
And they held prayer in the highest regards.
Ho na lé wačhékiyapi kiŋ lé iyótaŋȟčiŋ líla iyótaŋkilapi.
And so nowadays these generations don’t know, and they do things incorrectly, and they think that they do good things.
Ho čhaŋkhé leháŋn wičhóičhaǧe kiŋ lená slolyápi šni na, hé é táku ipáyeȟ ečhúŋpi na, hená táku wašté ečhúŋpi kéčhiŋpi.
So if they pray in Lakota they call the wanáǧi “spirits.”
Ho toháŋn Lakȟól’iya lená wačhékiyapi háŋtaŋhaŋš lená wanáǧi kiŋ “spirits” ewíčhakiyapi.
These spirits live on this here earth too so they help us.
Wanáǧi kiŋ lená íŋš-eyá makȟá kiŋ lél akáŋ úŋpi čha hená óuŋkiyapi.
So if a man puts down his life, and they put him in the earth, they pray for us, and in that way their spirits live on earth, and they help us.
Ho čha toháŋn wičháša waŋží wičhóni ókignakiŋ na, makȟá mahél iyéyapi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená wóčhekiye uŋkíčaǧapi héčhel tȟawóniya kiŋ lená makȟá akáŋ úŋpi na, hená óuŋkiyapi.
So we prayed like that then, so we never said anything, and in that way we couldn’t say anything.
Ho čha heháŋn lená héčhel wóčhekiye uŋkáǧapi čha, tákuni tóhaŋni uŋkéyapi šni na, héčhetu uŋkéyapi uŋkókihipi šni.
Way back one’s mother or father or grandmother or grandfather went around telling them stories, but they didn’t notice those things, and they didn’t listen to those things, so they were very happy.
Lená íŋš-eyá eháŋni húŋku na atkúkupi na kȟúŋšitkupi na tȟuŋkášitkupi kiŋ lená wóoyake owíčhakiyag awíčhaupi k’éyaš, takómni hená ablézapi šni na, hená naȟ’úŋpi šni čhaŋkhé, líla oíyokišiče.
And so nowadays we live on white people’s land, we live in big cities.
Ho čhaŋkhé leháŋn uŋk’úŋpi kiŋ lé ská makȟóčhe ektá uŋk’úpi, otȟúŋwahe tȟáŋka waŋ ektá uŋk’úŋpi.
Our Blessed Savior will be present in several things with peace.
Táku tóna Waníkiya uŋyáwaštepi kiŋ hená wóokiye él úŋ kte.
And we live around all that so it is difficult to pray in Lakota.
Ho na ektá óhaŋ uŋk’úŋpi čha lé Lakȟól’iya wóčhekiye kiŋ lená othéȟike.
There’s no place nor way to go into nature and pray.
Tukténi maníŋn uŋyáŋpi na wačhéuŋkhiyapi kta waníče.
Now they go around building houses, white people do, and there’s no nature left.
Hená áta oyáte kiŋ thikáȟ áyapi, hená ská oyáte kiŋ na, tukténi maníŋtu waníče šni.
And so even the animales live in nature, and so they’ve come to the city, and so they hit them, a lot of cars do.
Ho čhaŋkhé wamákȟaŋškaŋ kiŋ é kayéš lená maníŋn úŋpi yuŋkȟáŋ, lená otȟúŋwahe étkiya aú čhaŋkhé, kahíŋȟpewičhayapi, iyéčhiŋkyaŋke óta.
So they die miserably.
Čha úŋšišiya hená t’ápi.
They lay down its life miserably.
Hená úŋšišiya wičhóni ékignakapi.
And so if they make prayers, it is sad, and difficult.
Ho čhaŋkhé toháŋn wóčhekiye uŋkáǧapi hátaŋhaŋš, oíyokišiče na, othéȟike.
That is why we pray for them.
Lená uŋ wóčhekiye wičháuŋkičaǧapi.
In that way if those who lay down their lives, their spirits go back to the west and north and east and south, back to where the sun rises from, the east, then they say they reach up there.

Héčhel wičhóni ékignakapi kiŋ lená wiyóȟpeyatakiya na wazíyatakiya na wiyóhiyaŋpata na itókaǧa hená wanáǧi kiŋháŋ khiglápi háŋtaŋhaŋš, héktakiya wí hinápȟe héčhiyataŋ, wiyóhiyaŋpataŋhaŋ gliyáhaŋpi kéyapi.
And then it became dark, at night they say that the spirits walk on the road lies north and south that lies across the sky.
Ho na heháŋn aíyokpaze, haŋhépi ektá wazíyata naháŋ itókaǧata wanáǧi tȟačháŋku waŋ eyápi čha maȟpíya ektá glakíŋyaŋ ȟpáya čha hé ogná mánipi kéyapi.
So He will be there in peace at the big conference that Sisítȟuŋwaŋ people are going to have.
Hó lé tȟokáta Sisítȟuŋwaŋ omníčiye tȟáŋka yuhápi kte él lé wóokiye yaŋkíŋ kte.
So they often walk along that, and somehow they see the things we do down here, so if they don’t pray for us, they say they’re sad.
Čha hé ogná šna hená iyúha mánipi na, tókhel hukhúta waéčhuŋk’uŋpi kiŋ lená waŋúŋyaŋkapi čha, takómni wačhéuŋkiyapi šni háŋtaŋhaŋ, hená čhaŋtéšičapi kéyapi.
So they live and they can’t help us.
Čha úŋpi na óuŋkiyapi okíhipi šni.
In that way whenever we have a sweat lodge, and we pray, whenever they come back to here, we feed the spirits.
Héčhel toháŋn iníuŋkaǧapi na, wačhéuŋkiyapi čháŋšna, hená ektá hípi čháŋšna, hená wanáǧi wówičhauŋkič’upi.
In that way they walk freely in any direction.
Héčhel okáblaya tókhiya ománipi kte.
And if we ask for peace, they help us.
Na toháŋn wóokiye uŋlápi hátaŋhaŋš, óuŋkiyapi.
In that way we won’t suffer, and we will have a happy life, and we will have good health.
Héčhel uŋkákižapi kte šni na, wičhóni wašté uŋyúhapi kte naháŋ, wičhózani wašté uŋyúhapi kte.

So nowadays what we consider to be the most important thing is meekness, and is compassion, so if we definitely stand carry those two things with us in that way they will help us in what we ask of Creator.

Ho čha hé leháŋn táku waŋ líla iyótaŋȟči iyótaŋuŋlapi kiŋ hé wówaȟwala eyápi na, wówauŋšila eyápi čha henáos takómni waš’ágyahaŋ gluhá naúŋžiŋpi háŋtaŋhaŋš, héčhel táku Tȟuŋkášila uŋkílapi ešáš hená óuŋkiyapi kte.
In that way we give thanks, and we asking for something, so at least help us.
Héčhel wóphila uŋkéyapi na, ho akhé takún uŋlápi čha, ešáš akhé óuŋkiyiapi kte.
But if we are asking for something without anything, they won’t help us.
Ho tkȟá áyecechola táku uŋlá-haŋpi hátaŋhaŋš, tóhaŋni hená uŋkókihipi kte šni.
It is because of that that Lakota people run around as if lost living, and drinking strongly.
Hé é čha uŋ Lakȟóta oyáte kiŋ leháŋn núni s’e wičhóuŋ na, wayátkaŋpi kiŋ líla š’agyáhaŋ íŋyaŋke.
Look out well.
Taŋyáŋ abléza po.
And they don’t think about anything and they forget themselves.
Ho na tákuni él éwačhiŋpi šni na él éič’iktuŋwaŋpi šni.
All of them just like that, just drinking, they think that they are living healthily but it’s not like that.
Hená iyúha hógna ečéla, wayátkaŋ hé ečél uŋ, zaníya úŋpi kta kéčhiŋpi éyaš héčhetu šni.
That’s why in the old days they gave us these pieces of advice.
Hená eháŋni wówahokuŋkhiye kiŋ lená uŋk’úpi čha.
My myself, I really stand holding onto those things.
Hená miyé é wičákȟeyahaŋ glús nawážiŋ.

In that way my mother and father and grandfather and grandmothers’ spirits will have nicely walked making the journey, and so it’s me who lives suffering on this earth, but I definitely help the people, so they will help me back, too.

Héčhel iná é na até na tȟuŋkášila na uŋčíwičhawaye kiŋ lená héčhel wanáǧi oómani káǧapi k’uŋ hená iyókiphiya mánipi kte čhaŋkhé, miyé é makȟá kiŋ lél akáŋ kakíšya waúŋ tkȟá, takómni oyáte kiŋ ówičhawakiya čha, íŋš-eyá héktakiya hená ómakiyapi.
So I say thanks using those and in that way I honor them.
Čha hená uŋ wóphila epȟíŋ naháŋ héčhel wičháwagluonihaŋ.
In just that way I will be healthy, and the people should just do those things in order to be healthy.
Hógna ečéla mazáni kte na, hógna ečéla oyáte kiŋ zánipi kta čha uŋ lená ečhámuŋ.
And so I’m as unhappy as can be when people don’t go to pray.
Ho čhaŋkhé toháŋn okíhilaka iyómakiphi šni toháŋn oyáte kiŋháŋ wačhékiye yápi šni.
Also they pray at white churches, but that’s no big deal because they pray to Creator, too.
Nakúŋ ská owáčhekiye čha ektá wačhékiyapi éyaš, hé tókȟa šni ičhíŋ íŋš-eyá hená Tȟuŋkášila čhékiyapi čha.
Also they pray in English, so that’s no big deal, but if they pray in Lakota our relatives will hear us so they will help us so that’s why we pray in Lakota.
Íŋš-eyá hé wašíčuiyapi čhékiyapi čha, tókȟa šni, ho tkȟá Lakȟól’iya-haŋ wačhékhiyapi háŋtaŋhaŋ, uŋkítȟathitakuyepi kiŋ lená naúŋȟ’uŋpi kta čha óuŋkiyapi kta čha hé uŋ Lakȟól’iya-haŋ wačhéuŋkiyapi.
I greet you all with all my heart.
Čhaŋtéwašteya napéčhiyuzapi.
In that way we will accomplish things.
Hógna táku kiŋ lená uŋkókihipi kte.
So if they really go, and they stop drinking and smoking marijuana, and they go into a sweatlodge, and they dry themselves, then this would be a great cause for celebration.
Ho čha iyótaŋš iyáyapi naháŋ, wayátkaŋpi na pȟežúta šíča ičúpi kiŋ lená ayúštaŋpi naháŋ, oínikaǧe waŋ él thimá iyáyapi na, ikpákhiŋtapi háŋtaŋhaŋš, toháŋn okíhilaka hé wóphila tȟáŋka héčha.
And if they walk in that way, then we will walk along what they call the red road.
Na hé ogná mánipi háŋtaŋhaŋš, lé čhaŋkú waŋ lúta eyápi kiŋ lé hé ogná maúŋnipi kte.
But for example someone who walks along the black road drinks, and murders people, and steals, and all these bad things happen.
Ho tkȟá tuwá čhaŋkú waŋ sápa čha ogná iyáya ešáš wayátkiŋ na, thíwičhakte na, wamánuŋ na, táku šíča lená iyúha íŋyaŋke.
All of that because they live according to white people’s ways.
Hená ská wičhóuŋ kiŋ ogná wičhóuŋpi čha hé uŋ.

If they followed along with that, when we grew up ourselves, then we would listen to the parents’ words, so we lived well, but nowadays the people growing up don’t do that, so we are stuck with misery.
Hé ogná otȟápȟapi háŋtaŋhaŋš, uŋkíye uŋkíčhaǧapi kiŋháŋ tȟáŋkake kiŋ lená oíye nawíčhauŋȟ’uŋpi čha, taŋyáŋ uŋk’úŋpi éyaš, leháŋn ičháǧe kiŋ héčhuŋpi šni čha, wókakiže tȟáŋka ikȟóyaka.

So often for that reason I’m sad when all those Lakota people drink, and they don’t care for themselves, and some of the people who are maturing look very good, but they drag themselves around dirtily, like their face was melting off.

Čha eyášna uŋ čhaŋtémašiče toháŋn Lakȟóta kiŋ hená iyúha itómnipi na, él éič’iwačhiŋpi šni na, húŋȟ iyótaŋš lečhála ičháǧe kiŋ lená líla húŋȟ owáŋyaŋg waštéštepi éyaš, áta ité kiŋ šló aú sékse ománipi kačégčeg, šabyéla.
So in the old days the mother and fathers loved them, and so I say that around here they live not being concerned with themselves
Čha lená eháŋni húŋku na atkúkupi kiŋ thewíčhaȟilapi yuŋkȟáŋ, léčhiya él éič’iktuŋwaŋpi šni čha, úŋpi k’uŋ epȟé.
So from here on if the people live well, that would be very admirable.
Ho čha letáŋ tȟokátakiya lená oyáte kiŋháŋ taŋyáŋ úŋpi háŋtaŋhaŋš, héčhel wóphila tȟáŋka héčha kte.
So yeah.
Ho.
And a lot of the white people’s way of doing things are awful.
Na táku wičhóȟ’aŋ wašíču ečhúŋpi kiŋ óta theȟíke ló.
So nowadays people who are maturing now pray with something, and the things they will trust in are called an eagle feather, and a pipe, and the sweatlodge, and hoops in the four directions.

Ho čha leháŋn lečhála ičháǧe kiŋ lená táku uŋ wóčhekiye káǧapi naháŋ, uŋ lená wičálapi kte kiŋ hé waŋblí wíyaka waŋ hé é naháŋ, čhaŋnúŋpa waŋ hé é naháŋ, iníkaǧapi kiŋ hé é naháŋ, čhaŋgléška waŋ tȟatúye tópa čha eyápi.
So that is life.
Čha hé wičhóni héčha.
And Lakota people often make prayers with white sage, and sweetgrass, and juniper, or herbs.
Ho hé é naháŋ pȟežíȟota naháŋ, wačháŋǧa naháŋ, ȟaŋté naháŋ lená iyúha naíŋš, Lakȟóta pȟežúta kiŋ lená uŋ wóčhekiye eyášna uŋkáǧapi.
So this eagle feather, old-time Lakota people went on visionquest and some people did sacred things and so birds are called winged-beings.
Ho čha hé é waŋblí wíyaka kiŋ lé, eháŋni Lakȟóta kiŋ hená iháŋblapi na húŋȟ wakȟáŋȟ’aŋpi yuŋkȟáŋ ziŋtkála waȟúpakoza eyápi.
So eagles are considered very important.
Čha hé waŋblí kiŋ hé iyótaŋȟčiŋ waŋkátuya yawápi.

So it’s that, the wings that they take, and they pray with them, and the eagle is like the human, but before they do that, they bring them inside the sweatlodge, and they cry, and they dry it off, and if they leave with it, then they pull out the feathers, and they take the tail feathers, and they make use of them, and also the wings.

Ho hé é čha wíyaka kiŋ hé ičúpi na, yuhá wačhékiyapi naháŋ, waŋblí kiŋ hé wičháša iyéčhečapi éyaš, héčhuŋpi šni itȟókab, lé ziŋtkála kiŋ lé iníyothi thimá éyayapi na, wačhékiyapi na, pakhíŋtapi na, ho yuhá glinápȟapi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hó heháŋn wíyaka kiŋ hená yužúŋpi naháŋ, siŋtúpi kiŋ hená ičúpi na, hená wóilagyapi naháŋ, nakúŋ ȟupáhu kiŋ hená.
And they make use of the plume, too.
Ho na wáčhiŋhiŋ kiŋ hená nakúŋ wóilagyapi.
Lakota people used all of them for something.
Hená iyóhila Lakȟóta kiŋ táku uŋ wóilagyapi.
So they respect them.
Čhaŋkhé hená ohókilapi.
Crier
Éyaŋpaha
But nowadays they use some of them for no reason, and whenever they kill them, they lay them down in a cold way [in a freezer].
Éyaš leháŋn otúyačhiŋ húŋȟ wičháuŋpi na, wičháktepi čháŋ, sniyáŋ wičháuŋpapi.
And then the pipe comes from the earth, Grandmother Earth.
Ho naháŋ heháŋn čhaŋnúŋpa kiŋ lé makȟá etáŋ, Uŋčí Makȟá etáŋ hí.

So they take a rock from over there in the west at red stone quarry, and they make a pipe, and they smoke using those, and they take an ash tree, and before it cracks they break off something, and they peel it, and they dry it, and they straighten it out until it’s dry.

Čha he íŋyaŋ kiŋ hé ká wiyóhiyaŋpatakiya íŋyaŋ šá oók’e čha héčhiyataŋhaŋ ičúpi na, čhaŋnúŋpa káǧapi naháŋ, hená uŋ úŋpapi naháŋ, hé pséȟtiŋ kiŋ ičúpi naháŋ, našléče šni háŋni, kaksápi na, kaǧápapi naháŋ, pusyápi na, yuówotȟaŋ khuwápi na ečhél púze.
So in the middle of that there, I don’t knowhow they used to do that in the old days, but whenever they burn that pit, that’s stuck in the center, there’s a hole that they make a pipe from that.
Ho čha hé iyókogna kiŋ hél ogná, eháŋni tókhel léčhuŋpi kiŋ slolwáye šni, éyaš hená čhoǧíŋ waŋ čhokáŋ ikȟóyaka čha, hená ǧuyápi čháŋ, oȟlóka čha, hé čhaŋnúŋpa káǧapi.
So they fill it all with tobacco, and they ask Creator for peace, or they give thanks to Creator.
Čha hé é iyúha opáǧipi naháŋ, Tȟuŋkášila wóokiye kilápi naíŋš, wóphila ekíyapi.
In that way people are useful.
Ho hé uŋ hená wíyokihipi.
And meanwhile maybe if they’re sad, or if they suffer from something, [that person] will burn medicine, or sweetgrass, or juniper.
Ho naháŋ hé ičhúhaŋ lená uŋgnáš iyónikiphišni naíŋš, táku iníčakiže háŋtaŋhaŋš, lená pȟežíȟota kiŋ lé é naíŋš, wačháŋǧa kiŋ lé é naíŋš, ȟaŋté kiŋ lená zilyáyiŋ kte.
They’ll burn it and pray with it.
Zilyáyiŋ na uŋ wačhéyakiyiŋ kte.
In that way the relatives from way back will come and help us.
Héčhel eháŋni otákuye kiŋ lená hípi na óuŋkiyapi kte.
They do what we asked of them.
Hená táku uŋlápi k’uŋ hená ečhél héčhuŋpi.
We have the best of churches.
Thípi wakȟáŋ waŋží iyótaŋ wašté ȟča uŋyúhapi.
So they will make things right for us, so that’s why Lakota people never lived on this Earth for just no reason at all.
Ho uŋkíčiyusupi kta čha uŋ hená čha, Lakȟóta kiŋháŋ tóhaŋni otúyačhiŋ makȟá kiŋ lél akáŋ úŋpi šni.
If they kill something, then they leave, and they set up tobacco, and they pray over it, and they eat it.
Táku ktépi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená iyáyapi na, čhaŋlí waékignakapi na, awáčhekiyapi na, ho hená yútapi.

So the tobacco comes from kinnikinnick, so that comes from Grandmother Earth, and if the smoke rises up towards where Creator sits in heaven, then for that reason there’s peace, so that’s why the people pray like that.

Ho čhaŋlí kiŋ lé čhaŋšáša kiŋ hé etáŋ úŋ čha, hé uŋ Uŋčí Makȟá etáŋ hiyú na, Tȟuŋkášila waŋkáta maȟpíya ektá yaŋké kiŋ ektá étkiya šóta kiŋ lé izíte háŋtaŋhaŋš, ho hená uŋ wóokiye čha hé uŋ, hená héčhel wačhékiyapi.
So it’s not done in vain but they use some of it for a specific reason.
Ho čha táku kiŋ lená otúyačhiŋšni éyaš húŋȟ otúyačhiŋ wóilagyapi.
And then there’s a wheel with a certain quality that’s called a medicine wheel so that wheel is round so they dye the quills red, and they decorate around it with porcupine quills.
Ho na heháŋn hé čhaŋgléška waŋ ikȟóyaka čha hé pȟežúta čhaŋgléška eyápi ho čha hé čhaŋgléška kiŋ miméla čha, pȟahíŋ lulyápi na, ohómni óskapi.
And a cross is stuck in the middle so it is like the cross that white people pray, too.
Na čhaŋíčhipaweǧa waŋ čhokáŋ ikȟóyake čha hé íŋš-eyá lé wašíču wačhékiyapi kiŋ hé čhaŋíčhipaweǧa waŋ uŋ wačhékiyapi kiŋ lé íŋš-eyá iyéčheča.
But they pray up to Grandfather and Father Creator in Heaven by sticking a feather in the middle of a cross that goes to the west and north and east and south.

Ho éyaš uŋkíye hé čhaŋíčhipaweǧa kiŋ wiyóȟpeyata na wazíyata na wiyóhiyaŋpa na itókaǧa ho na čhokáŋ wíyaka waŋ ikȟóyaka čha hé uŋ Uŋčí Makȟá naháŋ Tȟuŋkášila Até Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka maȟpíya ektá hená uŋ wóčhekiye uŋkáǧapi.
So we don’t use those things for just any reason, so Lakota people pray around in a circle because the people’s way of life is circular.
Čha hená otúyačhiŋ wóilag’uŋyaŋpi šni čha, Lakȟóta oyáte kiŋ lená lená wičhóuŋ kiŋ miméyela čha okáwiŋȟ wačhékiyapi.
I suppose that it goes around from the west and north and east and south like that, and in that way it arrives back to the west.
Hé itȟó wiyóȟpeyatakiya na hetáŋ wazíyatakiya na wiyóhiyaŋpatakiya na itókaǧatakiya okáwiŋȟ héčhel yíŋ na héčhel héktakiya wiyóȟpeyatakiya khihúŋni.
And a house, a tipi that they lived in, those are circular, too.
Ho na thípi, thiíkčeya othípi kiŋ, lená nakúŋ miméyela.
We were very thankful for that at first.
Hé tȟokáheya wóphila tȟáŋka uŋyúhapi.
So nobody ever lived in a square way.
Ho čha tóhaŋni tákuni oblótȟuŋ šni.
So for that reason the sweat lodge is circular, too.
Čha héčhel hé iníyothi kiŋ hená nakúŋ miméla.
So they say that Lakota people never lived in a square way.
Čha hená Lakȟóta kiŋháŋ tóhaŋni oblótȟuŋyaŋ thípi šni kéyapi.
In that way they would pass on by in a circle without any obstructuion and they would come back.
Héčhetu wičhóuŋ kiŋ lé okáblaya okáwiŋȟya hiyáyapi na ečhél glihúŋnipi kte.
Using that all the things were circular.
Hé é čha uŋ táku kiŋ iyúha miméyela.
Or the birds’ nests are in a hoop, too.
Naíŋš nakúŋ ziŋtkála kiŋ hená hoȟpí tȟáwapi hená nakúŋ čhaŋgléška.
They live in a circle.
Miméyela wičhóthi.
Or Lakota people made use of all those types of hoops, none of those were ever squares.
Naíŋš táku óta čhaŋgléška hé Lakȟóta wóilagyapi, hená tóhuŋweni waŋžíni oblótȟuŋ šni.
So for that reason they respected them.
Čha hé uŋ hená ohókilapi čha.
If Lakota people lived knowing those things, then they will live good.
Lakȟóta kiŋháŋ hená ablésya úŋpi háŋtaŋhaŋš, líla taŋyáŋ úŋpi kte.
For that reason, I’ll say it like this.
Hé uŋ, léčhel epȟíŋ kte.
So, that’s all.
Ho, henákeča.
Our church is very big, and it reaches up high, and inside a very large lamp shines yellow, and every day the bell is rung.
Thípi wakȟáŋ uŋkítȟawapi hé líla tȟáŋka na, líla waŋkátuya na, imáhel pȟetížaŋžaŋ zí waŋží líla tȟáŋka iyóyaŋbyiŋ na, aŋpétu iyóhila ȟláȟla waŋží kaȟlápi.
So in that way, my relatives, whenever you go to somewhere or come back, you all should look to that building.
Hó héčhel, mitákuyepi, tókhiya yaípi na yakúpi čháŋna, thípi kiŋ hé ayátuŋwaŋpi kta iyéčheča.
I’ll tell how it is that they make fire.
Tókheškhe pȟéta káǧapi kiŋ hé é čha oblákiŋ kte.

Whenever inner cottonwood bark that is split at the edge like threads is lit on fire, it’s rotted wood that they take, and they lay it down torn apart, and they lay the bark down around it in the same way, and they strike flint just like that against each other.
Pȟéta iléyapi kiŋ hé wáǧačhaŋ há iyókogna haȟúŋta s’e swaká čha hená é čháŋ, čhaŋpúŋpuŋ čha ičúpi na, yuptá égnakapi na, lé čhaŋhá kiŋ héčheča áta ohómni égnakapi na, lé wahíŋ héčheča uŋ íčhiyapȟapi.
And whenever they ignite it, it burns, so if it burns a little, they go laying twigs and large logs on it, and if that fire is big, if they set that wood upright, then the fire will burn really big.

Na kaíleyapi čháŋšna, ilá čha, kitáŋla ilé háŋtaŋhaŋ, čhaŋsákala naháŋ sáŋm čháŋ tȟaŋkíŋkiŋyaŋ akšú-haŋpi na, hé pȟéta kiŋ líla tȟáŋka háŋtaŋhaŋš, čháŋ tȟáŋka čha hená yuwóslaslal églepi háŋtaŋhaŋ, líla pȟéta kiŋ tȟáŋka ilé.
So they make fire just like that.
Čha héčhuŋ-s’e pȟéta kiŋ káǧapi.

If they plan on lighting a fire, they do it just like that, or maybe if they’re somewhere in the wilderness, they take that sort of buffalo grass, it’s called buffalo grass, and they lay it all together, and they lay dried buffalo chips all around it, and if they light that it burns just like that, and those are the things with which they make fire.

Toháŋn pȟéta iléyapi kte háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená héčhuŋ-s’e ečhúŋpi naíŋš, uŋgnáš maníŋn tuktél háŋtaŋhaŋš, lé pȟežíšaša čha hená buffalo grass ečíyapi čha héčheča hená ičúpi naháŋ, ptáya égnakapi naháŋ, lé tȟatȟúŋkče púza čha áta ohómni égnakapi na, iléyapi háŋtaŋhaŋš, héčhel ilé čha hená é čha uŋ čhethípi.
They also lived in the wild, but they never talked about it.
Nakúŋ maníŋn thípi éyaš, hená tuwéni tóhuŋweni oyáke šni.
Also, if it’s dark for example, you all should see that lamp.
Nakúŋ oíyokpaza ešáš pȟetížaŋžaŋye kiŋ hé ayátuŋwaŋpi kta iyéčheča.
But other Native peoples light their fires differently.
Éyaš Lakȟóta tȟókeča kiŋ hená tȟogyé pȟéta káǧapi.
But we did it only in that way.
Éyaš uŋkíye hógna ečéla ečhúŋk’uŋpi.
So then I will tell about how I remember them making weapons or tipi poles or arrows with wood.
Lé ho heháŋn táku čháŋ uŋ wípȟe naíŋš, táku tȟušú thípi tȟušú naíŋš, wahíŋkpe kiŋ káǧapi kiŋ tókhel weksúya héči lé oblákiŋ kte.
Somebody who doesn’t have any land dies between the houses.
Tuwá makȟóčhe ničá hená thiwókhitȟahena t’é ló.
Also, if it’s awfully hot for example, you all should be able to hear that bell.
Nakúŋ kȟáta oíyokišiče ešáš ȟláȟla kiŋ hé anáyaǧoptaŋpi kta iyéčheča.
First for the arrows that they made, they took willow twigs or maybe wood that they picked up.
Tȟokéya wahíŋkpe káǧapi kiŋ hé, lé čhaŋsákala čha willow naíŋš, uŋgnáš čhaŋpáhi načhéče.
So they took them, they took them all straight, and they went along straightening them, and they dried them.
Čha hená ičúpi naháŋ, owótȟaŋla kiŋ hená ičúpi na, yuówotȟaŋ khuwápi na, pusyápi.
They did that, and they took willow, and they moistened it, and they stripped a feather, and they wrapped it around a tail.
Héčhuŋpi na, tȟakȟáŋ čha ičúpi naháŋ, yuspáyapi naháŋ, lé wíyaka kiŋ hé yusléčapi naháŋ, siŋté ektá iyápehaŋpi.

So they wrapped the feather around at the end, so there at the end, they cut a notch, and they moistened the sinew there, and they wrapped it around, and maybe whenever they applied pine gum or tender hooves, it was dry and stiff.

Čha hé iháŋke ektá wíyaka iyápehaŋpi čha, hél iháŋke él waškítapi na, hél ogná tȟakȟáŋ kiŋ lená yuspáyapi na, iyápemnipi na, hená lé uŋgnáš waŋží čhaŋší naíŋš, táku tȟašáke lolóbyapi héčheča iyúŋpi čháŋšna, šéče na, sáka čha.
In that way it wouldn’t get uncoiled.
Héčhel naglá šni.
So they wrapped those things around it and on both sides the wrapped feathers around it.
Čha hená él iyápemnipi naháŋ itȟánuŋgya wíyaka kiŋ hená iyápemnipi.

And then they applied a little of it on the big end of the wood, and they split it down the middle, and they stuck the flint in the middle, and then they stuck it in, and there cut in a groove, so they wrapped sinew around that too, or they stuck it on it like that.

Ho na heháŋn lé čháŋ kitáŋla tȟáŋka kiŋ ečhíyataŋhaŋ čha hé iyúŋpi na, čhokáŋ wasléčapi naháŋ, lé wahíŋ kiŋ hé iyókogna iyéyapi na heháŋn, toháŋn iyéyapi naháŋ, hél waškítapi čha, hógna íŋš-eyá hé tȟakȟáŋ iyápemnipi naíŋš, iyéčhel iyáskabyapi.
So if someone was really skilled at it, then fasten it straight, and for that reason they said that they were a good shot.
Ho čháŋšna hená é čha tuwá wayúphike háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená owótȟaŋla ikȟóyagya čha, uŋ waŋtáŋyeya kéyapi.
And they went hunting, and they killed animals with those things, and they came back with meat.
Na hená wayé yápi na, hená uŋ wamákȟaškaŋ wičháktepi na, tȟaló kiŋ aglípi.
And then next in the old days here was called a war club so those were smoothe stones and some were black and some were white.
Ho na heháŋn íyokhiheya hél íŋš eháŋni íŋyaŋ kapémnipi eyápi čha hená íŋš íŋyaŋ čha lé íŋyaŋ šlušlúta čha húŋȟ sápiŋ naíŋš húŋȟ ská.
As you know, that Catholic Church alone is really important, our Lord’s Word sits inside, and we should go to where it is that the light, bell, and priest appear, and we should listen to them.

Iŋčhíŋ Šinásapa Wóčhekiye hé išnála líla tȟáŋka, imáhel Itȟáŋčhaŋ uŋkítȟawapi hé Oíye yaŋká na, iyóyaŋpa kiŋ hé é na ȟláȟla kiŋ hé íŋš wičháša wakȟáŋ hé épi héčhel tókhiyataŋ hó tȟaŋíŋpi kiŋ étkiya uŋyáŋpi iyéčheča na, anáwičhaǧoptaŋpi kta iyéčheča.
So they took those rocks, and they made a hole in the middle of them some way, and they use them as a handle.
Čha hená íŋyaŋ kiŋ ičúpi naháŋ, tókheškhe čhokáŋyaŋ yuȟlókapi naháŋ, čháŋ ihúpayapi.

And they made a hole in the middle of a stone, so they push it into it, and from there it’s sinew that they take, and they take it wrapping it around the stone, and whenever they fix it at the bottom, then it’s really hard, so they didn’t knock it loose with those, so they made it like that.

Na íŋyaŋ waŋ čhokáŋ yuȟlókapi čha, hél opázaŋpi na, hetáŋ lená táku tȟakȟáŋ é čha hená ičúpi naháŋ, hená íŋyaŋ kiŋ opémni ičúpi naháŋ, khútakiya lé čháŋ kiŋ ogná iyáskabyapi čháŋšna, hé líla sutá čha, hená uŋ kašlókapi šni čha, héčhel káǧapi.
Or some people sewed wrapping around the stone with hide, and whenever they made it hard, they defended themselves with those warclubs, and whenever there was a battle, they used them, the men did.
Naíŋš húŋȟ tȟahá čha íŋyaŋ kiŋ hél aópemniyaŋ akáyeǧepi naháŋ, sutáya káǧapi čháŋšna, hená íŋyaŋ kapémnipi kiŋ uŋ naíč’ižiŋpi na, okíčhize čháŋ hená úŋpi, wičháša kiŋ.
It’s said that they’d knock them into a sitting position.
Tȟóka kiŋ kaȟpá wičháyaŋkapi kéye.
So they named them “whirling rocks.” [warclubs]
Ho čha hená héčhel íŋyaŋ kapémnipi eyá čhažéyatapi.
And they made all more sorts of things from that so some made them with beaded handles.
Ho naháŋ hetáŋ táku isáŋm káǧapi kiŋ hé očháže iyúhaȟčiŋ čha húŋȟ pšitȟó ihúpa káǧapi.
But they just made those for show.
Éyaš iŋšé hená wópazo uŋ káǧapi.
And they didn’t call arrows arrows, what they called them, I don’t remember, but that’s why they made some sort of weapon, too.
Naháŋ wahíŋkpe wahíŋkpe eyápi šni, tókhel eyápi, wéksuye šni éyaš, hená íŋš-eyá hé táku wípȟe čha hená káǧapi čha.
That thing had a very long handle, and at the end of it they attached a big arrow, so they called that a spear.
Íŋš-eyá hé é čha líla ihúpa háŋske na, wahíŋkpe waŋ tȟáŋka čha íŋkpa ektá ikȟóyagyapi čha, hé wahúkeza eyá čhažéyatapi.
Or if they chased someone they stabbed them with it, or they stab them with those things by hand.
Naíŋš tuwá khuwápi háŋtaŋhaŋš, uŋ čhapȟápi naíŋš hená uŋ íŋš-eyá napíkčeya čhapȟápi.
So, my relatives, you all know that things are like this, and you see them, and you hear them, and you learn them.
Hó, mitákuyepi, lená léčhetu čha slolyáyapi na, waŋlákapi na, nayáȟ’uŋpi na, uŋspénič’iyapi.
They don’t shoot them.
Khutépi šni.
They kill animals with them.
Hé é uŋ hená wamákȟaškaŋ wičháktepi.
So they make those things like that and then they make tipi poles there.
Čha hená héčhel káǧapi naháŋ heháŋn hél thípi tȟušú káǧapi.
So they chop them off too, and if the wood is still damp, then they peel the bark off with their hands.
Čha hená íŋš-eyá kaksápi na, toháŋ čháŋ kiŋ hená naháŋȟčiŋ spáye háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená áta há kiŋ yuȟláyapi.

They never peel it off with a sharp object, they peel it off with their bare hands, so they take it all off, so if they finish peeling it, it’s all slippery, then they tip it over and over, and if it’s dry, then in that way not a single one was bent.

Tóhaŋni kaskúskupi šni, hé é napíkčeya yuȟláyapi čha, áta há yušlóka-haŋ čha, šlušlúlyela šna áta yuȟlá yuštáŋpi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená yuptáŋyaŋ khuwápi na, púze háŋtaŋhaŋš, héčhel waŋžíni kawíŋže šni čha, héčhel káǧapi.
So they made those to put up tipis with, or if they took them down, then if a long time ago they all travelled walking around, they tied them to dogs or horses on both sides.
Čha hená uŋ thiíkčeya pawóslal iyéyapi čha káǧapi naíŋš, hená toháŋn yuȟpápi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená toháŋn eháŋni iglág wičhómani háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená šúŋka naíŋš šúŋkawakȟáŋ hená itȟánuŋg iyáwičhakaškapi.
So those dogs pulled those kids along, or they pull along parfleche bags, and they tied the tipi poles to the horses, so if there was a child or someone who was dying, they sat back there.

Čha šúŋka kiŋ hená wakȟáŋyeža hená wičháyuslohaŋpi naíŋš, táku wókapȟaŋ hená yuslóhaŋpi na, šúŋkawakȟáŋ kiŋ lená íŋš hená tȟušú kiŋ él iyáwičhakaškapi čha, hená íŋš wakȟáŋyeža naíŋš tuwá húŋkešni eháŋtaŋhaŋš, héktata yaŋkápi.
So it was the tipi covers that they rolled up, and they made it like a chair in the back so it was that they they dragged along.
Čha thiákaȟpe kiŋ hená é čha átaya pagmúpi na, héktataŋ oyáŋke s’e káǧapi čha hé é čha wičháyuslohaŋpi.
So they just did things in those sort of ways.
Čha iŋšé hená ečhékčhe waéčhuŋpi.
And if they put up a tipi, they treated the wood in a sacred way, so they didn’t break it by walking and pulling it around on the ground for a long time.
Naháŋ toháŋn ithíkaǧapi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená čháŋ kiŋ wakȟáŋyaŋ kičhúwapi čha, waŋžíni kawéǧe šni líla tȟéhaŋhaŋ yuslóhaŋ ománipi.
Then at the least, those who are Catholics in South Dakota, the only thing for you all to watch out for is earthly pride.
Héčheče ešáš, South Dakota imáhel Šinásapa yaúŋpi kiŋ makȟá wówitaŋ kiŋ hečéla akhítapi.
So if someone didn’t make a tipi well, and if they didn’t look after it, then it’s said they broke them.
Čha hená tuwá thípi kiŋ taŋyáŋ káǧapi šni na, čháŋ hená awáŋglakapi šni háŋtaŋhaŋš, kawéǧa kéye.
This is what we will learn from you all not looking towards God’s glory.
Na Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka tȟówitaŋ kiŋ eyátuŋwaŋpi šni hé uŋ táku waŋ uŋslólyapi kte kiŋ hé lé é.
People from the United States made a very big and beautiful boat and also it was very fast, they made it with a whole lot of money written down for it.
United States wičháša kiŋ wáta waŋží tȟáŋka wašté káǧapi na nakúŋ líla lúza, hé líla mázaska wóyawa tȟáŋka óta uŋ káǧapi.
And then there is a certain procedure for making bows and arrows.
Ho heháŋn lé itázipa naháŋ wahíŋkpe káǧapi kiŋ lená iŋšé wičhá tȟawóečhuŋ.
For that reason, it went along crossing the ocean in a couple nights.
Hé uŋ haŋhépi čónala mniwáŋča ópta oámani.
So they make a bow from an ash tree.
Čha hé pséȟtiŋ čha uŋ itázipa káǧapi.
They take a young ash tree, and they cut it, and that’s why there’s no branches.
Pséȟtiŋ tȟéča čha ičúpi naháŋ, kaksápi naháŋ, lé alétka waníča čha.
They cut it to where there’s no more branches, and they whittle the wood, and bend it, and it goes along drying.
Tuktél alétka waníče hétu čha kaksápi na, čháŋ kiŋ lé wažípapi na, yuktáŋpi na, púza áya.
That’s how it dries, so in that way the handle there is still round and they shave it on both sides, so that’s why they can bend it.
Ečhél pusyápi čha, héčhel oyúspe kiŋ hél héčhena gmigméla na itȟánuŋg wazízipelapi čha hé uŋ, yuktáŋpi okíhipi.
So they take it and it’s sinew that they twist two of together and they make rope out of them.
Čha ičúpi naháŋ lé tȟakȟáŋ čha hená íčhiyugmupi na hená ikȟáŋ káǧapi.
And the arrows are kinnikinnick but they’re a different type of kinnikinnick, but they’re not red, they’re yellow, so they take those, and make arrows out of them.
Ho naháŋ wahíŋkpe kiŋ hená íŋš lé, táku, čhaŋšáša hé é čha éyaš tȟókeča čhaŋšáša éyaš, šá šni, zí, čha hená ičúpi naháŋ, wahíŋkpe káǧapi.

And they pull the bark off of those too and they straighten and straighten them and on the big side they stick a piece of flint and then on the other side, the side of the tale, they split a feather and they shave it so using sinew they stick it to it wrapping it around and maybe they apply pine resin or boiled hooves.

Na hená íŋš-eyá há yuǧápapi naháŋ, yuówotȟaŋ khuwápi na, lé tȟáŋka ečhíyataŋhaŋ wahíŋ kiŋ hé ikȟóyagyapi na heháŋn, uŋmá ečhíyataŋhaŋ, siŋté ečhíyataŋhaŋ, hé wíyaka waŋ yuzápi naháŋ, kak’óǧapi čha, tȟakȟáŋ uŋ iyáskabya aíyapehaŋpi naháŋ, uŋgnáš wazí čhaŋší naíŋš tȟašáke piȟyápi.
They still applied it to it, so in that way it doesn’t unroll itself, and they say it’s really strong.
Héčheča iyútȟaŋtȟaŋpi čha, héčhel naglá šni na, líla sutá kéyapi.
So they do that, and in that way they shot some up using those things, so they made really straight sticks from those, so nobody made them quickly just because.
Čha héčhuŋpi na, hená uŋ húŋȟ waŋtáŋyaŋ yeyápi čha, hená íŋš-eyá čháŋ kiŋ owótȟaŋla ȟčiŋ káǧapi čha, tuwéni hená otúyačhiŋ káȟ iyéye šni.
They were looking over them until they made and finished them so that they would shoot things correctly.
Lená iwáŋyaŋka-haŋpi na ečhél taŋyáŋ wakhútepi kta héčhel hená káǧapi na yuštáŋpi.
In that way, only the very wealthy people were able to be there, and none of the poor people were able to be there.
Héčhel wičháša wížiča tȟáŋka kiŋ hená ečéla él yaŋkápi okíhipi na, wičhaša waȟpániča kiŋ hená tuwéni él yaŋká okíhi šni.
So that’s why, using arrows and bows, they went hunting or if they fought, they would use them.
Čha lé uŋ, wahíŋkpe na itázipa kiŋ lená uŋ, wayé yápi naíŋš toháŋn kičhízapi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hená él úŋpi.
So a long time ago the men were very strong so they would run next to buffalo and shoot them and hit them.
Čha lená eháŋni wičháša kiŋ líla waš’ákapi čha tȟatȟáŋka kiŋ kaísakhibya wičháiŋyaŋkapi na wičháopi.
And whenever they would shoot them, whenever they would sever what was a big artery lying there, they couldn’t move.
Na wičháopi čháŋ lé hél kȟáŋ tȟáŋka waŋ ȟpáya čha, hé é čha wopsákapi čháŋšna, iyáyapi okíhipi šni.
So they ran, and usually whenever they would stab them in the throat, they say that they would kill them back there.
Čha íŋyaŋkapi našná, loté kiŋ él očháwičhapȟapȟapi čháŋšna, éna t’ápi kéyapi.
And that’s the story.
Na héčhel wičhóoyake.
That’s all.
Henákeča.
In that way they travelled with their intense pride.
Héčhel hé wówitaŋ tȟáŋka uŋ ománipi.
They said that the boat would never sink.
Hé wáta kiŋ tóhaŋni mnít’iŋ kte šni kéyapi.
By plum shooting game they mean plum seeds.
Kȟaŋsúkhutepi eyápi hé hená kȟáŋta sú čha hená kȟápi.
So they took those and they brun them in many different ways.
Čha hená kȟáŋta sú kiŋ hená ičúpi naháŋ oštéšteya ǧuyápi.
And whenever they put them down and hit them, if someone wins, then they come and bet using maybe some beaded strings.
Ho na hená é čha napé él okígnakapi na kaslóhaŋ yeyápi čháŋšna, tuwá ohíye háŋtaŋhaŋš, tókhetu čha uŋgnáš pšitȟó oyázapi čha, hená uŋ ahíglepi.
So whenever they come and bet the old women sit together and they play the plum shooting game.
Čha hená ahíglepi čháŋ winúȟčala čha ptáyela yaŋkápi na hená kȟaŋsúkhutepi.
So that is one of the games.
Čha hená hé oškáte kiŋ waŋží.

And then there’s sliding-game where they sharpen an ash tree sapling about this long [6 feet] on the thick end of the stick, so it’s that that they dried straight, so it is that that they put on their own foot, and whenever they’d shove it and make it slide, then it’s said it went up and pierced into the ground somewhere.

Ho na heháŋn hél waŋží paslóhaŋpi eyápi čha hená íŋš lé pséȟtiŋ sakála čha, iŋšé hé toháŋkčakča čha háŋskaska čha, hená lé čháŋ kiŋháŋ lé tȟáŋka ečhíyataŋhaŋ kapȟéstopi čha hé é čha tókheškhe yuówotȟaŋ pusyápi čha, hé é čha sí kiŋ akáŋ ékignakapi naháŋ, woȟtákapi na woslóhaŋ iyéyapi čháŋšna, waŋkátakiya kiyíŋ na tókhiyab šna kaótaŋ glihé čha.
And the land is expansive, but it is filled with white men.
Na makȟóčhe kiŋ otȟáŋkaya k’éyaš óhiŋniyaŋ wašíču ožúlaye ló.
So all of those wealthy people believed that.
Hó héčhel wičháša wižíča kiŋ hená oyás’iŋ wičálapi.
They have competitions so they push it along.
Hená akíčhiyapi čha hená hé paslóhaŋ iyéyapi.

And then they sew a hide ball that they call the hitting ball, and they took an ash tree branch that was still young, and they bend it, and whenever they heated it straight over the fire, they dried it, and bent it, so it didn’t crack like that, so if it was dry, then it was dry like a cane, so they pulled off the bark, and it was by using that that they ran jerking the ball along, so they call it ball hitting game.

Ho na heháŋn hél tȟápa kakȟápapi eyápi čha hé íŋš tȟápa kiŋháŋ tȟahá čha kayéǧepi naháŋ, pséȟtiŋ čháŋ čha hená naháŋȟčiŋ tȟéča waŋ héhaŋ ičúpi na, yuktáŋpi na, kiŋ hél aíyopteya ačhéthipi čháŋšna, héčhena yuktáŋyaŋ púze čha, héčhel nasléče šni čha, toháŋn púze háŋtaŋhaŋš, héčhena sagyé s’e púze čha, hená há yuǧápapi naháŋ, hená é čha uŋ tȟápa yukȟáb ičú íŋyaŋkapi čha, hená tȟápa kakȟápapi eyápi.
So they stood on both sides and competed.
Čha itȟánuŋg nážiŋpi na akíčhiyapi.
If someone ran fast attached to the ball, and they ran jumping along, and whenever they hit it between the two poles standing vertically.
Tuwá lúzahe háŋtaŋhaŋš, áta tȟápa kiŋ ikȟóyagyiŋ na, yupsíl iyéya íŋyaŋkiŋ na, uŋmáčhiyataŋ čháŋ núŋm paslál háŋ čha čhokáŋ iyéyapi.
So those win and that’s why they did that.
Čha hená ohíyapi čha hé uŋ héčhuŋpi.
And then there’s the spinning top game where they scrape off a piece of wood in a circle, and they polish it, and they made it with a sharp point.
Ho na heháŋn akhé čhaŋkáwačhipi eyápi čha hé íŋš čháŋ čha gmigméya paskúpi naháŋ, hená átaya pašlúšlutapi na, ho hé pȟéstoya káǧapi.
So they tear a hide, and they wrap it around it, and they make it dance on a drum.
Čha hé lé tȟahá čha hé yusléčapi na, iyápehaŋpi na, čháǧa ektá akáŋ kawáčhipi.
They hit it, and make it jump, and usually whenever they hit it repeatedly, then they make that piece of wood dance.
Kapsíl iyéyapi našná, áta yusáksakapi čháŋšna, hé čháŋ kiŋ hé kawáčhipi.
So that’s just a game for boys.
Čha hé iŋšé hokšíla wóškate héčha.

And there’s the hoop rolling game where they tie a circular twig, and they dry it like that, and they cut the piece of wood at such a length [two to three feet], and that’s why whenever they run rolling it along, if someone knocks it over, then they win.

Na čhaŋgléška pagmíyaŋpi eyápi čha hé lé čhaŋsákala čha miméya iyákaškapi na, héčhel pusyápi na, čháŋ waŋ toháŋkčakča kaksápi na, hé é čha uŋ pagmíyaŋ íŋyaŋkapi čháŋšna, tuwá hé kaúŋke háŋtaŋhaŋš, hé ohíya kéye.
They didn’t know that something was blocking the way, but then one day, they came across something that was blocking the way.
Táku khušéya úŋ kiŋ hé slolyápi šni kiŋ hé úŋ tkȟá, waŋná aŋpétu waŋ él táku khušéya úŋ kiŋ akhípȟapi.
So it is just a game for boys, so they make them like that.
Čha iŋšé hé hokšíla wóškate čha, hená ečhél káǧapi.
In that way, that ship bumped against a piece of ice and the impact blinded it.
Héčhel wáta k’uŋ hé čháǧa waŋ [ibóto] na [woǧúŋǧe].
Today I will tell a story about something that my grandma told me.
Ho heháŋl táku waŋží oblákiŋ kte kiŋ hé eháŋni uŋčíwaye waŋ lé wičhóoyake kiŋ omákiyake.
And so whenever a young woman had a family in the old days it was said that they watched over her.
Yuŋkȟáŋ eháŋni wikȟóškalaka waŋží thiwáhe él yuhápi čháŋšna, héčhel awáŋkiglakapi kéye.
And it was said that they wanted her to have a good marriage.
Naháŋ taŋyáŋ héčhel hiŋgnátȟuŋkhiyapi čhíŋpi kéye.
So it was said that they weren’t willing to part.
Čha héčhel kpaǧáŋpi šni kéye.
Then in that way, a terrible event happened to them, and it was an awfully horrifying event.
Héčhel waŋná wótheȟike uŋ íyaglepi na, líla wónihiŋčiye tȟáŋka.
And so if they did it like, that then one day a young man likes a young woman, or if he is pleased with her, then it was said he came for her.
Yuŋkȟáŋ héčhel ečhúŋpi háŋtaŋhaŋ, aŋpétu waŋží él kȟoškálaka waŋží wikȟóškalaka kiŋ lé waštélakiŋ naíŋš, iyókiphi háŋtaŋhaŋš, hiyóu kéye.
And so in that way he rode a horse and in that way he came bringing another one.
Yuŋkȟáŋ šúŋkawakȟáŋ waŋží héčhel akáŋyaŋkiŋ na waŋží héčhel kašká yús aú kéye.
And so that horse comes bringing the family, and he talks to the mother and father, and it was said that he asks them for their daughter.
Yuŋkȟáŋ hé šúŋkawakȟáŋ kiŋ hé thiwáhe él yuhá hí na, húŋku na atkúku kiŋ owíčhakiyake na, wikȟóškalaka kiŋ hé čhuŋwíŋtku kiŋ hé wičhákila kéye.
And it was said that he made her ride the horse.
Ho hé šúŋkawakȟáŋ kiŋ hé akáŋyaŋkekhiya kéye.
He came with the extra hourse.
Ho naháŋ šúŋkawakȟáŋ waŋ akábya ahí.
It’s said that he gave it to the family.
Hé thiwáhe kiŋ él wičhák’u kéye.
He made her ride the horse whenever and it was said that he brought her back there by leading the horse along.
Ho čháŋ lé akáŋyaŋkekhiyiŋ na kašká yús héčhel aglá kéye.
And then she would live with their family like that so that’s how it was said that he arrived back with her.
Ho hé waŋná thiwáhe tȟáwapi ektá héčhel waŋná kičhí úŋ kta čha héčhel akhí kéye.
He arrived back with her and then afterwards it was said that there was an event.
Akhí naháŋ ho hé íyohakab hél wóečhuŋ yaŋká kéye.
But back then I was a girl, so I didn’t understand those things that well, and I wasn’t aware of them, so I’ve lost that story.
Éyaš hená héhaŋ wimáčhiŋčala čha, taŋyékel táku kiŋ lená owákaȟniǧe šni na, awábleze šni čha, heháŋl wičhóoyake kiŋ hé é wagnúni.

In the meanwhile two priests were there, and some men in Heaven saved them, and in the meanwhile there were some tiny boats there, and they said something like this right then into their ears while saving them:

Ečhúŋhaŋ wičháša wakȟáŋ núŋp él úŋpi na, wičháša uŋǧé maȟpíya él niwíčhakhiyapi na, íŋš ečhúŋhaŋ wátala eyá čikčístila él mahél úŋ na, hená íŋš-eyá wičhánuŋǧe niwíčhakhiya waŋná mahé táku iyáyapi k’él léčhel eyápi:
So that is all I will tell.
Ho heháŋyela oblákiŋ kte.
My God is near to me.
“Mitȟá-Wakáŋka mičáhda úŋ.
I am near to you.
Nikhíyela waúŋ.
He is near to me.
Mičáhda úŋ.
I’ll talk about old time Lakota people used to use cocklebur as medicine back in the day.
Héhaŋ táku waŋží oblákiŋ kte kiŋ hé wináwizitkȟaŋ hú kiŋ hé eháŋni Lakȟóta kiŋ pȟežútayapi.

And so that thing, being really good for healing kidney disease, they can’t pass that kidney sickness, they hold it in, and since they can’t pass it, on both sides of the long leaves of the bottom of this medicine it has long small leaves opposite of each other, so in the middle it has something prickly like an egg.

Yuŋkȟáŋ táku hé waŋ líla owášte kiŋ hé ažúŋtka wóyazaŋ kiŋ hé ihéyapi okíhipi šni, ihéyapi oglúspapi, na ihéyapi okíhipi šni kiŋ hé uŋ lé pȟežúta kiŋháŋ húta kiŋháŋ apé kiŋháŋ háŋskeya átaya itȟánuŋg léčhel apé kiŋháŋ čikčík’ala aíčhiyupteya háŋskeya ikȟóyaka čha, čhokáŋ táku wítka s’eléčheča pȟepȟé ikȟóyake.
They find it there, the medicine.
Ho hé oíyeyapi okíhipi, pȟežúta kiŋ lé.
Sometimes it grows along river banks.
Uŋgnáhaŋšna mayá aglágla ičháǧe.
So if they pull it up the roots are really long.
Ho hé yužúŋpi ehátaŋhaŋš hutkȟáŋ líla háŋskaska.
I stand at your cross.
Nitȟá-čhaŋsúsbeča kiŋ él ináwažiŋ.
It’s like the roots are yellow.
Hutkȟáŋ kiŋ hé zizí s’eléčheča.

So if they pull those long ones out, then they’ll cut them up, and peel them off, and they cut them up to a certain length, and it’s that that they boil with water, and they remove them well boiled (from the water), and then they cool off the water, and if it’s lukewarm, then they give it to whoever that person is in a bowl, so they recover from not being able to urinate, or having kidney pain.

Ho hé líla háŋskeya yužúŋpi hátaŋhaŋš, ho hé waksáksapi na, kaskúskupi naháŋ, toháŋhaŋ waksáksapi na, ho hé é čha mní uŋ piȟyápi na, mní waŋná taŋyáŋ píǧa-haŋ hená ȟeyáb ičúpi na, heháŋl waŋná mní kiŋ lé kasnípi naháŋ, ho t’ečá háŋtaŋhaŋš, ho wakšíča ogná tuwé kiŋ lé k’úpi eháŋtaŋhaŋš, ho hé lé ihéye šni naíŋš, ažúŋtka yazáŋ he uŋ akísni.

Akhípi naháŋke čha, “waŋ lé tókheškhe uŋktépi kte kiŋháŋ, uŋkókiyakapi éyaščhiŋ čhéǧa tȟáŋka uŋníčapi čha, tukténi tȟaŋkál čheúŋthipi uŋkókihipi šni čha, tókheškhe ečhúŋk’uŋpi kta he?” yuŋkȟáŋ uŋmá kiŋ é čha, “waŋ, microwave waŋ uŋyúhapi čha, héčhi mahél iyéyaye kiŋ oȟ’áŋkȟoya t’á iyáyiŋ kte,” eyá čha.
He said it and so, “okay, so let’s do that,” and then this turtle was still alive, but they still shoved it into the microwave.
Eyá čhaŋké, “oháŋ, čha héčhuŋk’uŋpi kte,” naháŋke lé khéyala k’uŋ héčhena ní k’éyaš, héčhena lé microwave kiŋ héčhiya pathímahel iyéyapi kéye.
And they closed the door, and so it really scratched with its feet inside, but they sat down in another room, and they sat watching TV.
Na thiyópa ečhél iyéyapi čhaŋké, áta mahél nak’éȟk’eǧe éyaš, thiyúŋmata íyutakapi na, TV waŋyáŋg yaŋká-haŋpi kéye.
And so someone knocked like that, so they opened the door, but there wasn’t anybody there, and so they said, “maybe somebody came then,” and they were sitting down.
Yuŋkȟáŋ léčhel tuwá katóto čha, thiyópa yuǧáŋpi éyaš, tuwéni šni čhaŋké, “tuwá lé hí séče éyaš,” eyápi na, yaŋká-haŋpi kéye.
Again someone knocked at the back door, so they looked over there, but there wasn’t anybody there.
Akhé thilázata thiyópa ektá tuwá katóto čha, ektá éwaŋyaŋkapi éyaš, tuwéni šni.
And so they were standing listening in the kitchen and so someone knocked again.
Čhaŋké olól’iȟ’aŋ thimá anáǧoptaŋ nážiŋpi yuŋkȟáŋ akhé katóto kéye.

And so it was the knocking sound that they followed, and so it was from the microwave that it came, and so they said, “well, it’s that turtle that we put inside that might be scratching,” and so they opened the door, and so they pulled the door open, and so it was that turtle that was carrying its turtle shell, and it crossed its legs, and was standing there leaning on the door and peering out, and it said, “all my relatives.”

Čhaŋké katóto kiŋ é čha owé otȟápȟapi yuŋkȟáŋ, lé microwave etáŋ čha ú čhaŋké, “waŋ, lé khéya waŋ lél mahél iyéuŋyaŋpi k’uŋ hé é čha nak’éȟk’eǧe séča waŋ,” eyápi yuŋkȟáŋ, thiyópa kiŋ yuǧáŋ ičúpi yuŋkȟáŋ, ečhél lé khéyala k’uŋ hé é čha khéya há kiŋ é čha alókiksohiŋ na, hukáičhičawiŋȟ lé thiyópa kiŋ él apútȟag ahíyokas’iŋ hinážiŋ na, “mitákuye oyás’iŋ,” eyá kéye.
“You two didn’t open up for a long time, it was really hot in there,” it said.
“Tókheškhe eháŋni ȟčiŋ luǧáŋpi šni, líla okȟáta škȟá,” eyá kéye.
“All my relatives.”
“Mitákuye oyás’iŋ.”
My relatives
Mitákuyepi
Our Savior didn’t live on the earth for no reason, but since he would complete everything, he suffered in thinking about everything for fourty days.
Waníkiya uŋkítȟawapi kiŋ otúyačhiŋ makȟá akáŋ ní šni tkȟá, táku oyás’iŋ yuštáŋ kte kiŋ hé uŋ aŋpétu wikčémna tóp él táku oyás’iŋ awáčhiŋ kakíže.
And we believe in Him, and when the time comes He will pray for us, as regards our souls.
Na Hé wičáuŋlapi na waŋná iyéhaŋtu k’uŋháŋ wóčhekiye waŋží uŋkíčaǧapi, uŋnáǧipi ečhíyataŋ uŋ.
So this story, a man joined the military.
Ho lé íŋš wičhóoyake kiŋháŋ, wičháša waŋ akíčhita ópȟa kéye.
And he was a soldier for three years.
Naháŋ waníyetu yámni akíčhita kéye.
So he was sixty-five years old then.
Ho na waŋná wikčémna šákpe sáŋm záptaŋ hinážiŋ kéye.
And He made a society for us.
Na okȟólakičhiye waŋží uŋkíčaǧapi.
And so he was confident in having a pension, so then he was ready to go there for that reason.
Yuŋkȟáŋ wóokiye ič’íla kta čha, waŋná yíŋ kta héčhel iglúwiŋyeya kéye.
And so they instructed him on it.
Yuŋkȟáŋ hé iyáksapapi kéye.
He said, “when you arrive, they will ask you a phrase first off so when they say, ‘how many years were you in the army?’ say, ‘three.’
“Ho lé yaí kiŋháŋ, tȟokáheya wičhóiye waŋží iníyuŋǧapi kta čha, ‘ho hé waníyetu tóna akíčhita oyápȟa he?’ eyápi kiŋháŋ, ‘three,’ eyá yo,” eyá kéye.
He said, ‘for three years.’
‘Hé waníyetu yámni yeló,’ eyá kéye.
And then they will say the following, ‘how old are you?’ so say, ‘sixty-five.’
Ho na heháŋl íyokhihe kiŋ hé íŋš, ‘waníyetu tonánikheča huŋwó?’ eyápi kta čha ho hé ‘sixty-five,’ eyá yo.
He said, ‘I’m that age.’”
‘Waŋná waníyetu henámakeča,’ eyá kéye.”
“Alright” he said.
“Tó” eyá kéye.
“I will surely say that,” he said.
“Tókša hé epȟíŋ kte ló,” eyá kéye.
Then he was going, and he got there, and so it was like there would be a white man that asked him how long it was that he was in the army that being the first question that he gave.

Waŋná yíŋ na, ektá í yuŋkȟáŋ, wašíču waŋ hé waŋná wóiyuŋǧe waŋ k’ú kiŋ hé tȟokáheya tuwá hé waŋná akíčhita ópȟa kiŋ hé waníyetu tónakeča ópȟa kiŋ hé iyúŋǧiŋ kte s’eléčheča yuŋkȟáŋ, tȟokáheya héčhel, “waníyetu tonánikeča huŋwó?” eyá kéye.
And so he said, “I’m three years old.”
Yuŋkȟáŋ, “waŋná waníyetu yámni henámakeča yeló,” eyá kéye.
Our bodies will be able to live well because of this.
Uŋtȟáŋčhaŋpi taŋyáŋ úŋ kte kiŋ hé uŋ.
“Three,” he said.
“Three,” eyá kéye.
So then he said, “how many years did you serve for?” and so he said, “sixty-five.”
Ho heháŋl, “waníyetu tóna akíčhita oyápȟa huŋwó?” eyá yuŋkȟáŋ, “sixty-five” eyá kéye.
So he asked him the other way around, so he said, “sixty-five,” and so he stared deep at him, saying that.
Ho hé uŋmáčhetkiya eyá iyúŋǧa čha, “sixty-five” eyá yuŋkȟáŋ, lílaȟčiŋ ayúta naháŋke, hé eyá kéye.
The white man said, “who’s crazy, you or me?”
Wašíču kiŋ, “who’s crazy, you or me?” eyá kéye.
“Who’s crazy, you or me?” he said, and so he said, “both.”
“Tuwá witkótkoka huŋwó, niyé naíŋš tókȟa miyé he?” eyá yuŋkȟáŋ, “both” eyá kéye.
He said, “if he says the question, ‘which do you want, clothes or money?’ say, ‘both.’”
“Ho hé nakúŋ wóiyuŋǧe waŋ eyé kiŋ hé, ‘tukté uŋmá yačhíŋ huŋwó, hayápi naíŋš mázaska?’ ehátaŋhaŋš, ‘both’ eyá yo,” héya kéye.
Well then it seemed like he said that, and so he asked wrongly, “who’s crazy, you or me?” and he said, “both.”
Ho tókhiŋš héyiŋ kte s’eléčheča yuŋkȟáŋ, ipáyeȟ wíyuŋǧa čha, “who’s crazy, you or me?” eyá yuŋkȟáŋ, “both,” eyá kéye.
Hear well what I have to tell you.
Wówašte uŋ wanáȟ’uŋ-čhičhíyape ló.
And he asks to take faith.
Na wówičala iču-úŋšipi.
He asks us to believe in something everlasting.
Táku owíhaŋke waníče kiŋ hé wičála-uŋšípi.
He chose twelve men.
Wičháša akénuŋp wičhákaȟniǧe.
So the old-time people didn’t know English in the slightest.
Ho eháŋni oyáte kiŋháŋ lílaȟčiŋ héčhel wašíčuiyápi šni.

And so they really couldn’t speak English, so a Chief would talk with a white man, so he knew parts of it, so he wanted him to translate for him, and so he said, “come here, translate for me, I’d like to talk with this white man.”

Yuŋkȟáŋ átayela wašíčuiya okíhipi šni čha, wičháša itȟáŋčhaŋ waŋ wašíču waŋ kičhí wóglakiŋ kta čha, lé haŋkéke slolyá čha iyékičiska čhíŋ naháŋke, “ho hiyú wo, iyémiyečiska yo, wašíču kiŋ lé kičhí wówaglakiŋ kta čha,” eyá kéye.
He lost his horse, so it was that that he wanted to ask about, and so he said, “talk for me, grandson, he said, ‘back where the first agency was located, I lost my red horse.’”
Ho hé šúŋkwakȟáŋ waŋ gnúni čha, hé é čha uŋ wíyuŋǧa čhíŋ naháŋke, heyá kéye, “ho omíčiyaka yo, tȟakóža, ‘owákpamni kiŋ lé tȟoká íyutaka héhaŋ, šúŋkawakȟáŋ waŋ híŋša čha wagnúni yelo,’” eyá kéye.
“Say that for me,” he said.
“Hé omíčiyaka yo,” eyá kéye.
And so the translator said, “when the first agency sit down he lost a red holy dog.”
Yuŋkȟáŋ iyéska kiŋ heyá kéye, “when the first agency sit down he lost a red holy dog.”
It was funny that he translated it into English like that for him.
Hé wašíčuiya iyékičiska kiŋ hé iŋšé hé wóiȟaka héčha.
It was funny him translating it as accurately as possible.
Eyá ognáye ȟčiŋ yuíyeska kiŋ hé é čha lé obláke wóiȟaka héčha.
It was like he said it wrong somehow, and so I said it as he said it for him just like that as precisely as possible.
Tuktógna ipáyeȟ eyíŋ kte s’eléčheča yuŋkȟáŋ, héčhuŋ-s’e iwáyuphiya okíčiyaka čha lé obláke.
He sent them to every people and they did it in all the ways in which our Savior asked them to do it.
Oyáte oyás’iŋ yewíčhaši na Itȟáŋčhaŋ uŋkítȟawapi kiŋ tókhel ečhúŋ-wičháši kiŋ oyás’iŋ ečhél ečhúŋpi.
According to that we all die, and from that only one died normally.
Ohnáyaŋ oyás’iŋ uŋt’ápi na, etáŋ waŋžíla ikčé t’é.

So nowadays they pin down the hide stretched out with them tanning hides, and they take what’s like black light weight motor oil, and they grease it with it, and if it doesn’t penetrate, then they apply it again

Ho lé tȟahá kpaŋyáŋpi kiŋ lé é čha leháŋn lečhála wičhóičhaǧe kiŋ lená tȟahá kiŋ hé yuzíl okátaŋpi na, átaya lé iyéčhiŋkyaŋke wígli sápa kap’óžela héčha čha ičúpi na, átaya uŋ slayápi naháŋ, kaȟlóg iyáye šni háŋtaŋhaŋš, akhé iyúŋpi.

And if it penetrates, then it’s like a washing machine that they throw it in with soap, and they wash it mixed up, and they wring it out, and so whenever they soften it by rubbing it, they soften it really well.
Na ho hé kaȟlóg iyáya háŋtaŋhaŋš, lé haíyužaža héčha čha, ektá haípažaža oíȟpeyapi na, ičáhi yužážapi na, yuškíčapi naháŋ, ho hená heháŋn yuȟúŋtapi čháŋšna, líla yuphíya šna yuȟúŋtapi.
So that is the modern way of doing it.
Čha íŋš hé lečhála wóečhuŋ.

And this being done with a sickle, they twist it with a clothesline, and they twist it with aluminum, and whenever they hang it loosely, whenever they soften it by rubbing it like that, it comes out soft and tender.

Na hená lé pȟežíkakse kiŋ lená héčhašniyaŋ, hená lé haíyotke kiŋ léčha čha yugmúŋpi na, mázaȟota héčha čha yugmúŋpi na, okáȟtagya lé otkéyapi čháŋšna, héčhel ečhúŋ hená yuȟúŋtapi čháŋšna, pȟaŋpȟáŋyela hináŋpȟe.
And way back there weren’t those things so nobody did that
Na eháŋni hená táku kiŋ waníča čha tuwéni hená héčhuŋ-he šni.
But nowadays there are all those things.
Éyaš leháŋn hená táku kiŋ iyúhaȟčiŋ yukȟé čha.
They do those things really quickly nowadays.
Iŋšé leháŋn táku ečhúpi kiŋ oȟ’áŋkȟokȟoya waéčhuŋpi.
And he is called St. John.
Na hé St. John ečíyapi.
When they gave Lakota people just flour and baking powder and grease, then they were really good at making bread.
Iŋšé lená lečhála Lakȟóta kiŋháŋ aǧúyapiblu naháŋ wínakapo na wígli kiŋ lená wičhák’upi k’uŋ héhaŋ, lená aǧúyapi kiŋ kaȟ wáyuphikapi.

Čha héhaŋ iŋšé wašíču eyá wašíču hiŋšmá ewíčhakiyapi čha hená aǧúyapi káǧapi čha, hená uŋspéwičhakhiyapi čha hé uŋ, hená héčhel káǧapi éyaš, isáŋm iyé iyáyapi naháŋ, wígli uŋ káǧapi.
And finally he made one of them into a preacher.
Na ehákeȟčiŋ wówahokuŋkhiye waŋží wičhákičaǧe.
So the hairy white people kneaded the bread that they made first of all, and they put it in what was a thick frying pan, and they applied the lid, and if they make a fire on it, the bread rises.
Čha hé tȟokéya aǧúyapi káǧapi kiŋ hé wašíču hiŋšmá kiŋ lená aǧúyapi paskápi na, maswíčheuŋpe šóka čha ektá mahél iyéyapi na, íyakaȟpe tȟúŋpi na, ačhéthipi háŋtaŋhaŋš, lé aǧúyapi kiŋ napóǧe.
And whenever it is cooked brown on both sides, they eat it by taking it and breaking it off with the hands.
Na itȟánuŋg ǧiyéla špáŋ čháŋšna, yuksáksa ičú yútapi.
Lakota people went and made frybread.
Ho éyaš lé Lakȟóta kiŋ iyáyapi na lé wígli uŋ káǧapi.
You will put about six handfulls of flour in it, and again you take about less than a handful, and you throw it on it.
Aǧúyapiblu tókhi napéyožula šákpe akhígle oyágnakiŋ kte naháŋ, akhé wínakapo kiŋháŋ tókhi napéyožulašniyaŋ iyókhiseyela iyáču na, él oyákala kte.
And throw on it a handfull of powdered milk and a pinch of salt.
Naháŋ asáŋpi blú kiŋ hé napéyožula naháŋ napépȟiŋkpa mniskúya oyákala kte.
And then you will mix in a very little bit of sugar, you’ll throw on it about two pinches of it.
Ho naháŋ čhaŋháŋpi kiŋ líla čónala íŋš ičáhiyayiŋ kte, napépȟiŋkpa núŋm wahénakeča oyákala kte.
You’ll still keep mixing it and with lukewarm water.
Héčhena áta iíčahiyayiŋ kte naháŋ mní sníšniyakel.
The water being lightly heated up, it isn’t very hot, but you will heat some water up easily, and you’ll put it on top of it.
Mní kiŋ kitáŋla akȟálya-ke s’e, líla kȟáte šni éyaš, mní etáŋ iwáštela kȟalyáyiŋ kte na, él oyákaštaŋ kte.
Do that, and mix it up, and if the flour gets thicker, then knead it.
Héčhanuŋ na, ičáhiyayiŋ na, toháŋn lé aǧúyapiblu kiŋ sáŋm šóka áye hátaŋhaŋš, yapát’iŋziŋ kte.

Knead it with the hands, and then cut it, and you flatten it with a rolling pin, and cut it up with a knife, and you check the oil’s temperature, and if it is hot, then you throw it on there, and if both sides are brown, then you flip it over, and if it gets brown, then it rises exactly the same on both sides and it is cooked.

Napé uŋ yapát’iŋziŋ na, ho luksíŋ na, aǧúyapi ipáblaye uŋ yapáblayiŋ naháŋ, míla uŋ wayáksaksa na, lé wígli kiŋ lé kȟal’ílutȟiŋ na, kȟáte háŋtaŋhaŋš, ektá oíȟpeyayiŋ naháŋ, uŋmáčhiyataŋ waŋná ǧí háŋtaŋhaŋš, ho luptáŋyiŋ naháŋ, ǧí áye háŋtaŋhaŋš, itȟánuŋgya ákhilehaŋyaŋ yuphíya napóǧiŋ na, špáŋ.
“Love everyone,” he often said.
“Oyás’iŋ waštékičhila po,” eyé s’a.
So they make bread, frybread, just like that.
Čha hená héčhuŋ-s’e aǧúyapi, wígli uŋ káǧapi, káǧapi.
Or they’ll also make it outside on the fire.
Naíŋš nakúŋ waŋží tȟaŋkál čhethípi héčhel yakáǧiŋ kte.
Also there is one that they call “baked bread.”
Nakúŋ waŋží čha hé aǧúyapi čhok’íŋ káǧapi eyápi.

So you also knead the dough, and it’s a skillet that you gently rub all over with grease, and you put it there, and if you kneaded it – if you kneaded it with your hands – and if it rises with a lid on, and you flip it over with it being brown on both sides, and you put the lid on it, and you’re about to gently put oil on it, then it cooks until being brown on both sides.

Čha hé íŋš-eyá aǧúyapi kiŋ yapáska naháŋ, lé maswíčheuŋpe héčheča ektá iwáštegla wígli iyákatȟaŋtȟaŋ na, oyágnakiŋ na, yapáblaye hátaŋhaŋš – napé uŋ yapáblaye háŋtaŋhaŋš – na íyakaȟpe yatȟúŋ kiŋ hé napóǧiŋ naháŋ, uŋmáčhiyataŋhaŋ ǧí kiŋ ho akhé luptáyiŋ na, íyakaȟpe yatȟúŋ yaglé na, iwáštegla wígli él oyágnakiŋ kte háŋtaŋhaŋš, yuphíya itȟánuŋgya ǧiyéla špáŋ.
So they call that baked bread.
Čha hená čhok’íŋ aǧúyapi eyá čhažéyatapi.
Lakota people make that.
Hená Lakȟóta kiŋ káǧapi.
Yup.
Kštó.
He would tell those words to the people many times over.
Óta akhígle wičhóiye kiŋ hé oyáte kiŋ owíčhakiyake s’a.
And so it was like a big evergreen tree that they often cut down, and whenever it was Christmas, they set it up in a church, and they take presents.
Yuŋkȟáŋ lé čháŋ wazíȟaŋte tȟáŋka héčheča hená eyášna kaksápi na, toháŋn Waníkiya Tȟúŋpi Aŋpétu čháŋšna, hená owáčhekiye él églepi na, wóšpipi.
So this church was a Lakota people’s church, so the people went to pray there, and anyone went there, and they prayed.
Ho čha lé owáčhekiye kiŋ lé Lakȟóta owáčhekiye čha, oyáte kiŋ hél wačhékiye yápi na, tuwé k’éyaš hél yápi naháŋ, wačhékiyapi.
Any kind of people.
Táku oyáte k’éyaš.

So they arrived there, and if they were about to cut down the tree, then they went to the mountains, and whenever they laid tobacco bundles and tobacco there, they chose that tree, and they laid tobacco around it, and they prayed.

Čha hená hípi na, toháŋn čháŋ kiŋ lé waŋná kaksápi kte háŋtaŋhaŋš, ȟé ektá yápi naháŋ, čhaŋlí wapȟáȟta na čhaŋlí héčhiya églepi čháŋšna, hé čháŋ kiŋ hé kaȟníǧapi na, ohómni čhaŋlí hená égnakapi na, wačhékiyapi.
And they prayed with the pipe, and they went knicking it with a boy or a girl.
Na čhaŋnúŋpa yuhá wačhékiyapi naháŋ, hokšíla waŋží naíŋš wičhíŋčala waŋží kičhí iyáyapi na, kahúŋpi.

They consider them sacred, so they went with them, and if they knick the tree, then they fell the tree afterwards, and they take it along making sure it doesn’t touch the earth, and they go back carrying it together, so afterwards it is around the base that they lay down ties of tobacco, and they pray, and they smoke over it, and then they come back to the building with it.
